# The Re-Enchantment of the World

> A study companion to Bernard Stiegler and Ars Industrialis, The Re-Enchantment of the World (2006; English 2014): layered summaries, concepts and evaluated sources.

A fair-use study companion to Bernard Stiegler and Ars Industrialis, *Réenchanter le monde.
La valeur esprit contre le populisme industriel* (Flammarion, 2006), translated by Trevor
Arthur as *The Re-Enchantment of the World: The Value of Spirit against Industrial
Populism* (Bloomsbury, 2014). It gives the thesis, a one-page overview, a summary of each
part from abstract down to section level with page numbers, concept pages, a glossary, the
book's reception, and evaluated third-party sources. It paraphrases and quotes briefly; it
does not reproduce the book. Each link below is the Markdown version of a page of
https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/.

# Start here

# Stiegler, *The Re-Enchantment of the World*: a study companion

*Bernard Stiegler &amp; Ars Industrialis, **Réenchanter le monde. La valeur esprit contre le populisme industriel** (Flammarion, 2006); **The Re-Enchantment of the World: The Value of Spirit against Industrial Populism**, trans. Trevor Arthur (Bloomsbury Academic, 2014).*

> A fair-use companion of condensed summaries, short attributed quotations and evaluated third-party accounts. It does **not** reproduce the book. Read it as a website at [lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/>).

## The thesis in one sentence

Consumer capitalism has captured desire and attention through the industries of communication and culture ("industrial populism"). In doing so it lowers "the value of spirit" and turns the promised knowledge society into a reign of ignorance. To re-enchant the world, the same technologies must become "technologies of spirit" that support knowledge, care and individuation, under an industrial politics led by a renewed public power.

## The book in one paragraph

In 2005 the French employers' federation, Medef, held its summer university under the slogan "the re-enchantment of the world" to promote the knowledge economy. Stiegler and the newly founded association **Ars Industrialis** "take it at its word". Re-enchantment requires reversing the "drop in the value of spirit" Paul Valéry noted in 1939. That drop is now organized by a **libidinal economy** in which television and marketing sell "available brain time". The result exhausts desire into drives and **proletarianizes** producers, consumers and knowledge workers alike, stripping them of *savoir-faire*, *savoir-vivre* and theoretical knowledge. Because human memory and knowledge have always been technical (**grammatization**, **tertiary retention**), the answer is not to reject technology. It is to invest, publicly and over the long term, in instruments, institutions and practices that let people re-appropriate their technologies of memory. The book gathers the association's 2005 manifesto (and, in English, its 2010 manifesto, which reframes the programme as a **pharmacology** of care and an **economy of contribution**), two essays by Stiegler on the "re-foundation of society" and "against the reign of ignorance", and a motion addressed to the 2005 UN summit on the information society in Tunis.

# Overview (L1)

[Home](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/index.md>) › **Overview** · down: [Structure](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/STRUCTURE/index.md>) · [Chapters](<#map-of-the-parts>) · [Concepts](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/GLOSSARY/index.md>)

*About a page. The argument arc, where the book sits in Stiegler's corpus, and the Ars Industrialis project. Evaluation is kept out of this file; see [reception.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/reception/index.md>).*

## 1\. What kind of book this is

*Réenchanter le monde* (Flammarion, 2006; English 2014) is not a treatise. It is the **founding dossier of Ars Industrialis**, the "international association for an industrial politics of technologies of spirit" that Bernard Stiegler set up in 2005 with George Collins, Marc Crépon, Catherine Perret and Caroline Stiegler. It contains:

- a polemical **Introduction** ("What Is to Be Done?", 2006);
- the association's **manifestos** (2005, and in the English edition only, 2010);
- two essays by Stiegler: **Ch. 1** "The Re-Foundation of Society" (2006) and **Ch. 2** "Against the Reign of Ignorance" (from a September 2005 talk);
- the **motion** the association published on the eve of the 2005 UN World Summit on the Information Society in Tunis.

Composition ran 2005 → 2006, plus a 2010 add-on, which is not the printed order. See [STRUCTURE.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/STRUCTURE/index.md>).

## 2\. The argument arc

1. **Provocation.** In 2005 the French employers' federation (Medef) took "the re-enchantment of the world" as the slogan of its summer university, to sell the "knowledge economy". Stiegler takes the slogan at its word. Re-enchantment would require raising the **[value of spirit](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/spirit/index.md>)**, the faculty Valéry saw falling in 1939. The milieu that coined the slogan is the one lowering that value. Its emblem is TF1's boast of selling "available brain time" to Coca-Cola. Stiegler's name for this is **[industrial populism](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/industrial-populism/index.md>)**.
2. **Diagnosis: libidinal economy and its exhaustion.** Twentieth-century capitalism organized consumption by capturing desire through the culture industries, a **[libidinal economy](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/libidinal-economy/index.md>)**. That capture has turned into its destruction: desire degrades into **drives**, sublimation fails, and attention is "short-circuited". The outcome is a **[symbolic misery](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/symbolic-misery/index.md>)**, and a **[disenchantment](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/disenchantment/index.md>)** more radical than Weber's.
3. **Mechanism: control of adoption and proletarianization.** **[Hyperindustrial](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/hyperindustrial-society/index.md>)** service capitalism controls how people *adopt* ways of life, and with it their **[individuation](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/transindividuation/index.md>)**. Knowledge is formalized into apparatuses and services and lost by individuals. Producers lose *savoir-faire*, consumers lose *savoir-vivre*, and knowledge workers lose theoretical knowledge. This is generalized **[proletarianization](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/proletarianization/index.md>)**.
4. **Ground: memory is technical.** Human memory and knowledge have always been externalized, through **[grammatization](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/grammatization/index.md>)**, **[tertiary retention](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/tertiary-retention/index.md>)** and ***[hypomnemata](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/hypomnemata/index.md>)***. The problem is not technology as such but whether a society organizes the **re-interiorization** of its memory technologies. Schools did this for writing. Today the **program industries** out-compete the program institutions.
5. **Contradiction of the "knowledge society".** Commodified information is **entropic**. Knowledge is **negentropic**. An economy that reduces knowledge to information risks a **reign of ignorance** ([knowledge vs information](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/knowledge-vs-information/index.md>)).
6. **Remedy: an industrial politics of spirit.** The same technologies are **[technologies of spirit](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/technologies-of-spirit/index.md>)**. They could support a new age of individuation if a **new public power**, working with industry and taking a long view against **[short-termism](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/short-termism/index.md>)**, invested in instruments of knowledge, reformed media and education, and championed a **European way of life**. Already in Ch. 1, and systematically in the 2010 Manifesto, this is framed as **[pharmacology](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/pharmakon/index.md>)**: every technics is both poison and remedy. It calls for an **[economy of contribution](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/economy-of-contribution/index.md>)** built on **[care](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/care/index.md>)** and **[associated milieus](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/associated-milieu/index.md>)**, and for reconquering free time as ***[otium](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/otium-negotium/index.md>)***.

## 3\. Place in Stiegler's corpus

| Period | Works (FR date) | Relation to this book |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Foundations | *Technics and Time* 1–3 (1994, 1996, 2001); *Echographies of Television* (with Derrida, 1996) | Originary technicity; epiphylogenesis; **tertiary retention**; *TT3* supplies the "prosthetic" synthesis, the adoption theory and the "ill-being" of cinema/TV that Chs. 1–2 rely on. |
| Political turn (2003–06) | *Acting Out* (2003); *Symbolic Misery* 1–2 (2004–05: "the hyperindustrial epoch", "the catastrophe of the sensible"); *Disbelief and Discredit* 1–3 (2004–06: decadence of industrial democracies; uncontrollable societies of disaffected individuals; the lost spirit of capitalism); *Constituer l'Europe* 1–2 (2005); *La Télécratie contre la démocratie* (2006) | **The book's immediate context.** Its vocabulary of symbolic misery, libidinal economy, the spirit of capitalism, disindividuation, Europe and telecracy is drawn from these, often in compressed form. Ch. 1's notes refer to *Disbelief and Discredit 2* and *Télécratie*. |
| **This book** | *Réenchanter le monde* (2006) | A popularizing, programmatic hinge. It turns the 2004–06 diagnoses into an **association** and a **policy agenda**. |
| Care and pharmacology | *Taking Care of Youth and the Generations* (*Prendre soin*, 2008); *For a New Critique of Political Economy* (2009); *What Makes Life Worth Living: On Pharmacology* (2010) | Systematizes what Ch. 1 already sets out: **care** as socio-therapy, the **pharmakon** (pp. 47–51) and the **economy of contribution** (pp. 36–37). The 2010 Manifesto (EN edition) belongs to this phase. |
| Late work | *States of Shock* (2012); *Automatic Society* (2015); *The Neganthropocene* (2018); *In the Disruption* (2016); *Qu'appelle-t-on panser ?* (2018–20) | Entropy/negentropy, first sketched in Ch. 2's knowledge/information contrast, becomes **neganthropology**. The contributory economy becomes the Plaine Commune contributory-income experiment. |

## 4\. The Ars Industrialis project

- **Founded** spring 2005 in Paris (manifesto; the association was active roughly 2005–2020). Public sessions were held at the Théâtre de la Colline and Centre Pompidou. It later ran working groups ("techniques of the self", "relational technologies", "economy of contribution"), a *Vocabulaire*, and the summer school **pharmakon.fr** (from 2010). It worked closely with the IRI (Institut de recherche et d'innovation, Centre Pompidou), which built contributory annotation tools such as *Lignes de temps*.
- **Self-image**: a research collective modelled, by its own account, on the early Frankfurt School, aimed at **public power and industry**, not at party politics.
- **Political register**: European, reformist, interventionist. It calls for a "new spirit of capitalism", not its abolition. Whether that is a strength or a weakness is a matter for [reception.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/reception/index.md>).

# Translator's Preface (Trevor Arthur), pp. vii–ix

[Home](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/index.md>) › [Overview](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/overview/index.md>) › [Structure](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/STRUCTURE/index.md>) › **Translator's Preface** · next: [Introduction →](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/chapters/01-introduction-what-is-to-be-done/index.md>)

## Abstract (L2)

A three-page note by the American translator. It explains two choices that shape how English readers meet the book: leaving ***savoir-faire*** and ***savoir-vivre*** untranslated, and the inadequacy of "spirit" for ***esprit***. On the way it gives a compact gloss of the book's problem: **industrial populism** proletarianizes us twice, as workers and as consumers. Its remedy is the **value of spirit**.

## Core claims

- The French is technically easy but syntactically intricate. Long nested clauses are kept where possible.
- ***Savoir-faire*** = the craftsman's, *techne*-bound knowledge. Losing it to machines is **[proletarianization](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/proletarianization/index.md>)**.
- ***Savoir-vivre*** = social grace and care for self and others (*politesse*, heard through *polis*). Losing it in the role of consumer is a second proletarianization. It is glossed through Simondon's **[individuation and transindividuation](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/transindividuation/index.md>)**.
- In consumer society desire is reduced to **drives**, sublimation is cancelled, and needs and wants are confused. This is the problem of **[industrial populism](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/industrial-populism/index.md>)**.
- ***Valeur esprit*** (no "of" in French). ***[Esprit](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/spirit/index.md>)*** joins the psychic, social, intellectual and historical. It is where memory and intelligence meet in reflection.

## Section-by-section (L3)

| pp. | Move |
| --- | --- |
| vii | Difficulty lies in style, not lexicon. Justifies leaving *savoir-faire* in French: its double sense of general practical wisdom and the specific skill of a *techne*. The worker "stripped of his savoir-faire" is proletarianized, and service industries now saturate personal life too. |
| viii | *Savoir-vivre*: the consumer relinquishes it and is "proletarianized all over again". Drives versus desire; sublimation; addiction ("addictive and toxic environment"). Introduces "industrial populism" and "the value of spirit" as the book's poles. |
| viii–ix | *Esprit* versus "spirit": common root *spiritus* (breath). *Esprit* as a synthesis tied to individuation ("one becomes who he is") and transindividuation ("we become who we are"). The closing image is of the world able to "sing again" through a revaluation of desire over drives and association over discord. |

## Notes

- **Interpretive (labelled):** the preface already frames the book in the *later* vocabulary of drives, addiction and care. That framing fits the 2010 Manifesto better than the 2006 chapters.
- The text has small typos ("contra", "le valeur", "Steigler", "savior-faire"). Reviewers such as Patrick Lyons (see [reception.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/reception/index.md>)) credit the preface with clarifying "spirit".

# Introduction: What Is to Be Done? (pp. 1–10)

[Home](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/index.md>) › [Overview](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/overview/index.md>) › [Structure](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/STRUCTURE/index.md>) › **Introduction** · prev: [← Translator's Preface](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/chapters/00-translators-preface/index.md>) · next: [2005 Manifesto →](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/chapters/02-manifesto-2005/index.md>)

## Abstract (L2)

The Introduction gives the book its title and its problem. In 2005 the French employers' federation, **Medef**, held its summer university under the slogan *"le réenchantement du monde"* to promote the "knowledge economy". The book "takes Medef at its word". To re-enchant the world through technologies of consciousness requires revaluing **[spirit](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/spirit/index.md>)** in the economy. The obstacle is that the same milieu (Seillière's preface to a book in which TF1's Patrick Le Lay boasts of selling "available brain time") organizes the **"drop in the value of spirit"** (Valéry, 1939) through an **[industrial populism](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/industrial-populism/index.md>)**. Twentieth-century capitalism is a **[libidinal economy](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/libidinal-economy/index.md>)** that, in capturing desire, destroys it. This is a chapter of Weber's **[disenchantment](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/disenchantment/index.md>)**. The ecological and demographic stakes of the coming decades demand "a new human consciousness". In short, humanity must overcome the **age of consumption** through a "new, qualitative growth", a "new industrial model" and a new **spirit of capitalism**.

## Core claims

1. The capitalism called "cultural" or "cognitive" is above all an **industrial populism** that uses every technical evolution to turn consciousness, "the seat of spirit", into a **reflex organ**. A brain without consciousness becomes a commodity on the audience market whose value keeps falling (p. 1).
2. Benjamin and Freud saw that communication technologies began a new history of consciousness and the unconscious. They did not see the organization of capitalism around the **consumer** as a **libidinal economy**, a channelling of desire. Benjamin saw the aestheticization of politics under fascism but not the **aestheticization of the economy** through control technologies and the manufacture of consumers (pp. 1–2).
3. This libidinal economy, by destroying consciousness, **destroys desire**. That is a chapter of Weber's **disenchantment** of the world (p. 2).
4. Medef's 2005 "re-enchantment" (Denis Kessler; Tony Blair's proposal to move EU agricultural funds to cognitive-technology R&amp;D) is ambiguous. It could be a genuine "jumpstart" of spirit, or the industrial production of **knowledge without spirit**, as one now produces "brains without consciousness" (pp. 2–3).
5. Ars Industrialis is "an international association for an industrial politics of technologies of spirit" (p. 3).
6. Humanity faces challenges (ecology, scarcity; Laurence Tubiana, Robert Lyon's "age of less") that require a new human consciousness and **overcoming the age of consumption** by "new, qualitative growth" (p. 3).
7. Contemporary capitalism replaces intelligence and responsibility with "the time of gregarious audiences" and nervous systems turned into reflex, i.e. **drive**, systems; consumerism has reached a "mortally toxic limit" (p. 4). Only a fight against industrial populism can re-enchant the world by making it **desirable** again and restoring reason as a *motive* for living (p. 5).
8. Medef's slogan alludes to Weber: capitalism unleashed disenchantment through a stroke of enchantment (the Protestant spirit, itself tied to the printing press, a "techno-logy" of spirit). Rationalization is then a new spirit that lowers the value of spirit. The present low point calls for a **sursaut** ("sudden surge") and a new spirit of capitalism (p. 5).
9. Capitalism, which "to this day does not have a credible alternative", can survive only by raising the value of spirit against industrial populism. That is why Ars Industrialis was founded (p. 6).
10. Spirit is a modality of **psychic and collective individuation** (Simondon). Knowledge is "the treasure bequeathed by those who are dead". The conditions under which a technology of spirit elevates rather than degrades spirit are a question of **political economy**, not to be left to shareholders. Public opinion must side with industrial capitalism against **financier capitalism**, "the true underwriter of industrial populism" (p. 7).

## Argumentative moves

- **Taking the adversary at its word.** The book does not reject the business slogan "re-enchantment". It radicalizes it, and turns it against those who coined it.
- **Juxtaposition as proof.** Seillière's knowledge-economy rhetoric and Le Lay's "brain time" appear in the *same* book (*Les Dirigeants face au changement*, 2004). Stiegler treats this co-presence as revealing the system's contradiction.
- **Genealogy by great names.** Valéry (value of spirit), Benjamin and Freud (technology and the psyche), Weber (disenchantment) and Derrida (*Echographies of Television*, 1993) locate the present as an unforeseen stage.
- **From culture critique to political economy.** The question "what is to be done?" is answered by founding an association and calling for an industrial politics.

## Section-by-section (L3)

The Introduction has no internal headings. It is divided by asterisks.

| pp. | Content (paraphrase) |
| --- | --- |
| x | **Epigraph, Ulrich Beck.** What industrial capitalism disenchants is pre-capitalist tradition, which keeps regenerating. Beck adds that this holds only until the 1950s. |
| 1 | **Valéry 1939.** "Drop in the value of spirit" on the eve of Nazism's catastrophe. **Derrida–Stiegler 1993** did not foresee **"libidinal television"**: reality TV soliciting the "scopic drive" (voyeurism/exhibitionism). **1939 → 2000s**: 45% radio listenership, no TV, to communication objects chasing "available brain-time" day and night. Cultural/cognitive capitalism = **industrial populism**; consciousness reduced to a reflex organ ("a slug's" neurons); brain time sold ever cheaper. |
| 1–2 | **Benjamin and Freud.** They saw the new history of consciousness and the unconscious but missed capitalism's reorganization around the **consumer** as a libidinal economy. They were preoccupied with fascism. Benjamin missed the **aestheticization of the economy**. |
| 2 | **Libidinal economy as disenchantment.** The organization of desire, which turned into its destruction by destroying consciousness, is a chapter of Weber's **disenchantment**. **Medef's 2005 summer university** was titled "The re-enchantment of the world": Kessler, cognitive capitalism, Blair's proposal on agricultural funds. To re-enchant through technologies of consciousness means revisiting the role of spirit in the economy. |
| 2–3 | **Seillière and Le Lay.** Seillière's preface to *Les Dirigeants face au changement* takes Kessler-like positions on the knowledge economy, and it introduces the very text in which Le Lay describes selling available brain-time, i.e. organizing the drop in the value of spirit, "the reign of stupidity". Dilemma: a jumpstart of spirit, or knowledge without spirit? Is knowledge possible without spirit at all? |
| 3 | **Ars Industrialis** defined. **Stakes**: humanity needs unprecedented intelligence and responsibility, or humans become "inhuman" (Jarry). Tubiana: the necessary change is so deep it seems unimaginable. Lyon: "the age of less", being rather than having. Survival requires overcoming the **age of consumption** through **qualitative growth**, not mere reduction. |
| 4 | To survive, humanity must **raise the level of intelligence**. Mental regression, moral debasement and the anaesthetizing of intelligence and will now govern the hyperindustrial world and the discourse of would-be governors. Program industries replace intelligence with "gregarious audiences" and drive-based reflexes for marketing. The consumerist model is suicidal. |
| 5 | Nearly all social life is controlled by the **industry of available brain-time**. Only a fight against this industrial populism can re-enchant the world, i.e. make it *desirable* and restore reason (Aristotle's *logos* and *noûs*, Valéry's "spirit") as the motive and orientation of existence. **Weber**: capitalism unleashes disenchantment through a stroke of enchantment (Protestantism, born of the printing press). Rationalization (reason as *ratio*, calculation) lowers the value of spirit and reifies reason (Lukács, Adorno, Horkheimer, Habermas). The extreme low calls for a rebound, a **sursaut**, i.e. "the invention of a new spirit of capitalism" (n. 10–11: against Boltanski &amp; Chiapello, *Le nouvel esprit du capitalisme*; see *Mécréance et discrédit*). |
| 6 | Capitalism will not survive without a new spirit and must fight what in itself secretes industrial populism. It "does not have a credible alternative", so it must open itself to an increase in the value of spirit. Since 9/11 television has become largely drive-based, with potentially tragic geopolitical effects. Against industrial and political populism, fanaticism and regression, and for a **new industrial model** with the value of spirit at the centre of its libidinal economy, Stiegler founded **Ars Industrialis** with George Collins, Marc Crépon, Catherine Perret and Caroline Stiegler. Radio, TV, computers and the internet are "spiritual instruments" (Mallarmé on the book): **hypomnemata**, which supported the "writing of the self" (Foucault) but also the sophists' manipulation of opinion. Philosophy was born fighting that and must now wage a new battle. |
| 7 | Ars Industrialis exists to find new philosophical "weapons" and political actions. Spirit, which always presupposes technologies of spirit, is a modality of **psychic and collective individuation** (Simondon). Knowledge, inherited from the dead, lets a society project and desire a future. When a technology of spirit elevates rather than degrades spirit is a question of **political economy**, "life or death for humanity", and must not be left to shareholders. Public opinion should back industrial capitalism against **financier capitalism**. Politics should frame economic initiative through social rules and **public investment**, via a **new form of public power**. A seminar, *Trouver de nouvelles armes*, ran at the Collège International de Philosophie from autumn 2005. |
| 8 | **Founding story**: asked "what is to be done?" at the Schaubühne, Berlin, in January 2005, Stiegler announced an association for 15 April 2005, ahead of the 29 May referendum on the European Constitution. The five founders shared an analysis of the constitution but disagreed about how to respond to the referendum. The website opened on 15 April 2005; the first plenary was held at the Théâtre national de la Colline on 18 June, where the 2005 Manifesto was presented. Later sessions covered **cognitive technologies**, the **Tunis summit**, **psychic suffering** from addictive consumption, and **television**. The two chapters are "reformulations and elaborations" of papers from the first two working sessions after the inaugural one. |
| 9 | The book closes with the **complete text** of the motion adopted a few days before Tunis, of which *Libération* published excerpts. Sessions resumed in October 2006 (a new public power; reorganizing education "from top to bottom"). At the same time Stiegler published *La Télécratie contre la démocratie. Lettre ouverte aux représentants politiques*, with proposals in his own name for the coming French election campaign. At stake is the role of France and Europe in "the survival of mankind". |
| 10 | Blank. |

**Introduction notes (pp. 101–102), complete gloss.**
