## E. Cross-source disagreements

| Issue | Positions | Our assessment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Is the remedy empty? | Lotz: "empty placeholders". Lyons: "philosophy of hope" but no concrete answers. Lemmens interview: a "new industrial model" with policy planks | Both reviewers under-weight the 2010 Manifesto §9 policies and Ch. 2's "practical consequences". Those are concrete but sectoral (education, media, R&amp;D instruments) rather than an account of political agency |
| Marx | Lotz, Hutnyk, Manche: class and accumulation sidelined. Ross, Lemmens: return to the *Grundrisse* and the knowledge sense of proletarianization | A real disagreement of frameworks; see [concepts/proletarianization.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/concepts/proletarianization/index.md>) |
| Spirit | Roodt: reduced to libido. De Beer: spiritual depth. Abbinnett v. Beardsworth: memorial v. futural. Rossouw: theological | The book's own definition is noetic and transindividual and explicitly not only religious (Tunis motion) |
| Digital networks | 2010 Manifesto: associated milieu. Stiegler 2018: "systemically dissociating" | The author revised his view; read the 2010 text historically |
| Authorship / founders | EN Wikipedia: three co-authors. Catalogues and association: five founders | Five (Collins, Crépon, Perret, B. Stiegler, C. Stiegler) |
| Tunis motion | Lyons, blurbs: "at the summit", "account of the summit". Association: press motion on the eve | The association's account is correct |

## F. Ranked reading list

Ordered by value for someone reading the book now. Primary texts first, because their accuracy is not in question.

1. **[primary-parallel-stiegler-colline-2005](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/primary-parallel-stiegler-colline-2005/index.md>)**: the draft of Ch. 2. Read it before or alongside the chapter.
2. **[primary-parallel-stiegler-uncontrollable-societies-nja-2013](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/primary-parallel-stiegler-uncontrollable-societies-nja-2013/index.md>)**: the best contemporaneous statement of spirit, Medef and industrial populism.
3. **[review-lotz-marx-and-philosophy-2015](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/review-lotz-marx-and-philosophy-2015/index.md>)**: the best page-located review, and the sharpest critique of the book itself.
4. **[lit-ross-neganthropocene-introduction-2018](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/lit-ross-neganthropocene-introduction-2018/index.md>)**: places the book in the corpus; the author's own later revision.
5. **[glossary-arsindustrialis-vocabulaire-2013](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/glossary-arsindustrialis-vocabulaire-2013/index.md>)**: house definitions. Mind the dating.
6. **[lit-manche-proletarianisation-not-capitalism-2021](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/lit-manche-proletarianisation-not-capitalism-2021/index.md>)**: the strongest critique of proletarianization and contribution.
7. **[lit-cohen-dare-to-care-2017](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/lit-cohen-dare-to-care-2017/index.md>)**: Valéry's *esprit* and care.
8. **[review-roodt-tydskrif-vir-geesteswetenskappe-2012](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/review-roodt-tydskrif-vir-geesteswetenskappe-2012/index.md>)**: the Arendtian challenge to "life of the mind".
9. **[lit-lemmens-digital-pharmakon-general-intellect-2017](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/lit-lemmens-digital-pharmakon-general-intellect-2017/index.md>)**: a sympathetic critique of statism.
10. **[primary-parallel-stiegler-pharmacology-of-desire-2011](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/primary-parallel-stiegler-pharmacology-of-desire-2011/index.md>)**: the libidinal-economy thesis at full strength.
11. [lit-abbinnett-politics-of-spirit-2015](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/lit-abbinnett-politics-of-spirit-2015/index.md>): the Derridean reading of spirit.
12. [review-debeer-tydskrif-vir-geesteswetenskappe-2012](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/review-debeer-tydskrif-vir-geesteswetenskappe-2012/index.md>): French page anchors.
13. [review-lyons-critical-inquiry-2014](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/review-lyons-critical-inquiry-2014/index.md>): the sympathetic Anglophone reception.
14. [context-le-lay-temps-de-cerveau-2004](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/context-le-lay-temps-de-cerveau-2004/index.md>) and [context-medef-universite-ete-2005](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/context-medef-universite-ete-2005/index.md>): needed to follow the Introduction.
15. [lit-hutnyk-proletarianisation-2012](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/lit-hutnyk-proletarianisation-2012/index.md>), [lit-hansen-saving-libidinal-capitalism-2014](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/lit-hansen-saving-libidinal-capitalism-2014/index.md>), [lit-hui-halpin-collective-individuation-2013](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/lit-hui-halpin-collective-individuation-2013/index.md>): further angles.
16. Everything else is reception colour or bibliographic support.

# Ars Industrialis 2005 Manifesto (web version)

The association's own English web version of the 2005 Manifesto, with the French original. The book reprints the manifesto at pp. 11–16 of the English edition. The web English is **not** Trevor Arthur's translation, so its wording differs from the book's.

## Condensed account

1. **Threat.** The "life of the mind/spirit" (Arendt) risks total subjection to the market. Firms exploiting the culture industries, program industries, media, telecoms and finally cognitive technologies drive this. Digitization makes these sectors **converge**, and the converged sector is named the **technologies of spirit**. Thesis: convergence has so far intensified *control*, but these technologies can and must open a new age of spirit.
2. **Industrial politics = industrial ecology of spirit.** Under market criteria alone the technologies of spirit serve **societies of control** (Burroughs → Deleuze). That means short-term financial return, and new social practices are blocked. Properly used, they could found a new epoch of civilization and avert a widely sensed chaos.
3. **Desire destroyed.** These technologies of "soul" and "consciousness", now joined by bio-technologies, aim to control modes of existence at every stage of life. Control of desire destroys the *singularity* that existing requires, and it destroys **libidinal energy** (Freud). Twentieth-century capitalism made libido its main energy source, channelled into commodities to absorb excess production. The capture of libido has ended up **destroying** it, which leads "inevitably" to an unprecedented global crisis.
4. **Super-ego and sublimation.** The ruin of desire is the ruin of **sublimation** and of the constitution of the super-ego. It brings geopolitical, political, social and psychic disorders on top of economic ones, under a model that sets production and consumption against each other.
5. **Singularity vs calculation.** Desire forms in symbolic practices supported by techniques. Objects of desire are singular. Industrial fabrication of desire *categorizes* singularities and makes the incalculable calculable. Yet singularity is not outside technics; art aims at "a number that averts counting" (Claudel). ICTs are **hypomnemata** (Foucault's "writing of the self"; Plato's *hypomnesis*). Like ancient hypomnemata they call for new practices and new social organization, not just user manuals and marketing for 15%-plus shareholder returns.
6. **Self-destructive capitalism.** "This capitalism is self-destructive." The association will fight the tendency by inventing practices of spiritual technologies that rebuild objects of desire and experiences of singularity.
7. **Boost desire, not consumption.** The political-economic task is to revive desire, not consumption. The general interest is a question of the symbolic, so a **new form of public power** is needed. It would join firms, public bodies, foundations, associations, economists, artists, scientists, philosophers and investors.
8. **Scope.** Based in Paris, European first, international in aim.
9. **Objectives and programme.** Symposia, publications, motions and studies. A Paris meeting series: European policy on industries of spirit; Google's digital-library initiative; research; the **Tunis WSIS (Nov 2005)**; marketing and advertising; art in industrial society; European languages and idiomatic difference; psychological disorders and public health; intellectual property; US, Latin American, Chinese and Japanese perspectives.

## Short quotations

- "This capitalism is self-destructive."
- The goal is "giving a boost to desire, and not simply giving a boost to consumption".

## Notes for evaluation

- The text is primary, so its accuracy is not in question. The interest is in its **predictive claim** (an "unprecedented global crisis"), which the 2010 Manifesto cites as vindicated by 2007–8.
- **Stance:** Freudian libidinal economy plus Foucault's hypomnemata and Deleuze's control societies. It is reformist and Europeanist ("new public power", with no anti-capitalist programme). This is the root of later charges of "technoreformism" (see [reception.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/reception/index.md>)).
- The web English is rough, with typos ("instrinsically", "Japn"). Quote from the Bloomsbury text rather than this version.

# Ars Industrialis 2010 Manifesto (web version)

The association's English web version of the 2010 Manifesto, with the French original. The English edition prints it at pp. 17–28; it post-dates the French book of 2006 (see [STRUCTURE.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/STRUCTURE/index.md>)). Its footnotes are unfinished placeholders ("Cf. Vocabulaire, p…"), so it is a working draft of the translation.

## Condensed account (by numbered section)

1. **Vindication and diagnosis.** The 2005 claim that capitalism had become self-destructive is confirmed by the 2007 subprime crisis. That crisis is not only financial. It is a crisis of the **consumerist model** founded (via Edward Bernays, Freud's nephew) on instrumentalizing desire, which ends by destroying desire. Destroyed desire means destroyed **investment** of every kind. The speculator, a capitalist who no longer invests, and the consumer are both **drive-based**, and their behaviour is systemically linked. **Disinvestment** is the effect of neoliberal **short-termism**. The result is "systemic stupidity" (*bêtise*).
2. **Disposability and addiction.** Consumer objects are made to be thrown away (Schumpeter's "creative destruction"). The waste is ecological, and it is also psychic: people who dispose of things feel disposable themselves. Consumerist society is **addictogenic** (the 2009 French addiction congress is cited). Addicts no longer take care of self, others or world, which produces a society of **carelessness** (*incurie*), a **dissociation**. Hence the axiom: *to economize means first of all to take care* (**care**).
3. **The economy of contribution.** The consumption-based model (early twentieth century, devised to overcome nineteenth-century productivism) has hit its limits through negative externalities: toxic assets, pollution, attention disorders, incivility, "the becoming-mafia of capital". It must give way to the **economy of contribution**, which produces **positive externalities** (care for self and others; Sen's **capabilities**). Free/open-source software is an example. On the net there are no longer producers versus consumers but **contributors** forming an **associated milieu** (Simondon). This restores sublimation and fights addiction.
4. **Pharmacology.** Social networks show hyper-consumerist behaviour that is even more mimetic. Reasons:
5. 4.1. Digital technologies are **hypomnemata**, and therefore **pharmaka** (Plato): poison and remedy.
6. 4.2. All technics is pharmacological. Without a therapeutic (*melete*, *epimeleia*: discipline, care, technique of the self) a pharmakon becomes toxic. Politics, and so political economy, is a **system of care**. Culture is what cultivates a caring relation to pharmaka.
7. 4.3. For two millennia *savoir-vivre* rested on **writing** as the pharmakon of reference (Scripture, humanities, Republic of Letters, press). It spread globally, including via Jesuit missions ahead of industrial markets.
8. 4.4. The culture industries (radio, TV) are new hypomnemata (Benjamin understood this; the Frankfurt School did not). They compete with **program institutions** (schools and universities). Reason is replaced by **rationalization** (Weber, Adorno, Marcuse, Habermas).
9. 4.5. Digital hypomnemata could end this, but marketing seized them first as **relational technologies**.
10. 4.6. Since Thatcher and Reagan, **public power** has renounced industrial policy, which is its proper role: turning "a technical becoming into a social future".
11. 4.7. This failure is "carelessness", with a risk of politico-military-ecological catastrophe.
12. **Political project.** Public power should support the emerging contributory model. Consumerism is hegemonic exactly at its limit. Responsible politics must secure the short term ("keep the wheels turning") *in order to* reach and reverse it in the long term. Each person is both a dependent consumer and a citizen. Consumerism is "in contradiction with the future" (100 million births a year). The goal is a **new industrial economy founded on care**, not "green consumerism". The passage runs from **disapprenticeship** (destroyed *savoir-faire*, *savoir-vivre*, theoretical knowledge; Madoff as symptom) to development of **capabilities**. The digital is a pharmakon that can deepen or end generalized **proletarianization**. Facebook had 500 million members in July 2010.
13. **Proletarianization defined.** It is the process by which knowledge formalized in a technique, machine or apparatus escapes the individual. Smith and Marx: workers lose *savoir-faire*. The twentieth century: consumers lose *savoir-vivre*, replaced by apparatus (the TV set) and services ("available brain time"). Now cognitive workers lose theoretical and critical knowledge, as in Greenspan's admission that he did not understand the system he ran. Free software is exemplary of **de-proletarianization**. **Psychotechnologies** must become **nootechnologies** (technologies of spirit).
14. **Generalization.** The model applies beyond the digital. "Light time" replaces "carbon time". **Smart grids** dissolve the producer/consumer split in energy, and AMAPs (community-supported agriculture) do the same for food. The ethics of contributory business is **care as political economy**. Local authorities should prioritize a pharmacology of networks and Sen-style "capacitation".
15. **Territory.** Relational technologies are localizable and serve **re-territorialization**. The end of consumerism is the end of globalization, giving **post-globalization**. Territory is the ground for political de-proletarianization (Pierre Veltz on learning regions).
16. **National policy (six planks in this web draft; the printed book has seven, adding a plank on rebuilding financial systems against speculation; see [chapters/03](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/chapters/03-manifesto-2010/index.md>)):** (9.1) scientific, technological and industrial policy for the new digital system; (9.2) education policy rearranging written knowledge with digital hypomnemata; (9.3) fiscal policy rewarding positive externalities, with work distinct from "employment"; (9.4) cultural policy as social investment and capacitation; (9.5) health policy on psychotechnological toxicity and non-drug addictions, read "pharmacologically" in Plato's sense; (9.6) media policy against **industrial populism**, restoring the press and program industries to forming public space.
17. **Programme.** Working groups on "techniques of the self"; contributive tools such as *Lignes de temps* (IRI software); work with Nantes Métropole and Nord-Pas-de-Calais; a research model likened to the early Frankfurt School.

## Short quotations

- "to economize means first of all and before anything else to take care" (§2).
- Consumerism, "as an organization of an innovation founded on disposability, waste, carelessness and blindness, … is in contradiction with the future" (§5; Lotz cites the Bloomsbury rendering at p. 23).

## Notes for evaluation

- **Primary.** It updates the 2005 text in the vocabulary of Stiegler's 2008–2010 books: pharmacology (*Ce qui fait que la vie vaut la peine d'être vécue*, 2010), care (*Prendre soin*, 2008) and the contributory economy (*Pour une nouvelle critique de l'économie politique*, 2009). The 2006 chapters already use **pharmakon**, **contribution** and **associated milieu** (Ch. 1, pp. 36–37, 47–51); the 2010 text makes them its frame. See [STRUCTURE.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/STRUCTURE/index.md>).
- The web draft's footnotes are incomplete. Use the printed Bloomsbury text for citations.

# The Tunis motion (French original)

The French text of the motion as *Libération* printed it on 14 November 2005, two days before the WSIS second phase (Tunis, 16–18 Nov 2005). It is an **excerpt**: per the book's Introduction (p. 9) and the motion's n. 1 (p. 112), *Libération* published part of it, and the book prints the complete motion (pp. 95–100; FR p. 163), roughly twice as long. The printed version adds the intellectual-property argument, numbered points, three conditions, Porto Alegre, the FCC model, Reding and the French government; see [chapters/06](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/chapters/06-tunis-motion/index.md>). The book's subheading "The true stakes of the Tunis summit" (p. 95) translates this page's title.

## Condensed account

1. The real stake of the "information society" is UNESCO's **knowledge societies**. The future of capitalism, and of the planet, depends on *raising* intelligence and knowledge. Knowledge is by essence shared and shareable. Digital cognitive and cultural technologies are reshaping the world's whole **public space**. Knowledge societies can arise there only if that space is regulated to serve people's capacity to discern, criticize, create, transmit and receive knowledge.
2. **Tunis is a missed appointment.** The UN summit will not ask the main question: how information, knowledge, technology, industry and society relate, as the object of an international policy to transform a **consumption capitalism** that now yields only **desublimation** and mental, moral, intellectual and aesthetic regression.
3. **Spirit is not (only) religious.** Faced with **spiritual misery**, people feel they need spirit. But spirit should not be placed only in religion and salvation. The life of spirit happens in daily work, relationships and communication tools, above all those reaching mass TV and mobile audiences.
4. **Call for another summit** built on an **industrial politics of technologies of spirit**. Spirit here means both the "available brain time" TV sells and the *œuvres de l'esprit* (works of mind). Valéry is quoted: a world transformed by spirit poses spirit entirely new problems.
5. **Means.** A new form of **public power** working with economic actors should turn ICTs into instruments for a new industrial model aimed at *raising* individual and collective intelligence. If the information society is to be a knowledge society, **television must become an instrument of knowledge**, not of **industrial populism**. Digital technology makes a different TV possible.
6. **Europe.** Europe can build itself on a forward-looking project in the knowledge and culture industries. Public and private funds that do not demand short-term returns should support real research. The model is medicine or physics. Spirit is now the first industrial resource after matter, so new solvencies and new fields of externalities are needed.
7. **New spirit of capitalism.** Planetary problems will force deep behavioural change, which requires sharper intelligences. The question of a "new spirit of capitalism" is posed. Social standard of living is measured by the quality of spiritual life, not protein consumed.
8. **Policy targets.** It welcomes the presidential commission to Jean-Louis Beffa for an industrial-policy report but says the report ignores technologies of spirit. The Barroso Lisbon strategy does not go in this direction. "Cultural diversity" is not enough: what is needed is industrial policy aimed at *raising* social life against **levelling**.
9. **Closing.** The state, the EU and industry must give Europeans hope in their culture again. What is singular to Europe since Greece is a **public space of knowledge**, now no longer only written but made of cognitive and cultural industries. "That is the stake of Tunis."

## Short quotations (translated by us)

- Television must become "an instrument of knowledge, and no longer the instrument of industrial populism that it has become".
- The rise in social living standards "is not measured by the quantity of protein consumed, but by the quality of the life of its spirit".

## Notes for evaluation

- **Primary.** It is the most compact statement of the 2005 position and shows that **industrial populism** was coined with **television** foremost in mind.
- It is strongly **Europeanist** and **state-plus-industry** (Beffa, Lisbon). There is no talk yet of contributory economy or pharmacology.
- On publication: the English book calls it "a motion adopted by Ars Industrialis", while the website says it was "published in Libération". An Ars Industrialis session on 24 Sept 2005 was explicitly held to draft it (see [primary-parallel-stiegler-colline-2005.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/primary-parallel-stiegler-colline-2005/index.md>)).

# Bloomsbury preview of the English edition

Bloomsbury's online sample of the English edition (14 pp.): front matter, contents, Translator's Preface and the opening of the Introduction. Its contents page gives the page numbers used in [STRUCTURE.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/STRUCTURE/index.md>).

## What it establishes

- **Bibliographic facts.** Bloomsbury Academic, London/New York, 2014. The book is in the series *Philosophy, Aesthetics and Cultural Theory* (series editor Hugh J. Silverman). The French original is given as *Réenchanter le monde* © Flammarion 2006. The English title page credits **Bernard Stiegler alone**, unlike the French cover, which reads "Bernard Stiegler et Ars Industrialis". ISBNs: pb 978-1-4411-6925-9, hb 978-1-4411-0346-8, epub 978-1-4411-5056-1, PDF 978-1-4411-6734-7. LC classification HD60.S83713 2014. The subject headings are "Industries—Social aspects" and "Technology—Social aspects".
- **Full table of contents with page numbers.** See [STRUCTURE.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/STRUCTURE/index.md>).
- **Translator's Preface (pp. vii–ix, Brooklyn, June 2013).** Condensed account:
- The translator found the vocabulary easy, with philosophical and technical Latin cognates, but the style hard. French allows long nested clauses, and he kept them where he could.
- He leaves *savoir-faire* and *savoir-vivre* in French. *Savoir-faire* is the craftsman's knowledge tied to a *techne*. Its loss to the machine is **proletarianization**. *Savoir-vivre* is social grace, care for self and others, and *politesse* heard through *polis*. It is lost when the person becomes consumer as well as worker, which he calls a second proletarianization. He links *savoir-vivre* to Simondon's individuation and transindividuation, as taken up by Stiegler.
- In consumer society desire is reduced to **drives**, sublimation is blocked, and wants and needs are confused. Arthur names this the problem the book calls **industrial populism**, and its antidote is the **value of spirit**.
- *Valeur esprit*: the French drops the "of". *Esprit* is broader than English "spirit". It joins the psychic, the social, the intellectual and the historical. It is tied to individuation ("one becomes who he is") and transindividuation ("we become who we are"), and to memory and intelligence meeting in reflection.
- **Epigraph.** A passage from Ulrich Beck: what is "disenchanted" in industrial modernity is pre-industrial tradition, which keeps regenerating. A second line then says this held only until the 1950s.
- **Introduction, pp. 1–3 (of pp. 1–10).** See [chapters/01-introduction-what-is-to-be-done.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/chapters/01-introduction-what-is-to-be-done/index.md>) for the condensed account. Key moves: Valéry's 1939 "drop in the value of spirit". The 1993 Derrida–Stiegler television conversation (*Echographies of Television*), which did not foresee "libidinal television"/reality TV. Radio reached 45% of French people in 1939; by the 2000s communication objects chase "available brain-time" day and night. "Cultural"/"cognitive" capitalism is in fact an **industrial populism** that turns consciousness into a reflex organ, and brain time is sold on the audience market. Benjamin and Freud saw the new history of consciousness but not the organization of capitalism around the **consumer**, a **libidinal economy** that, by destroying consciousness, destroys desire. All this is a chapter of Weber's **disenchantment**. Medef's 2005 summer university was titled "The re-enchantment of the world" (Denis Kessler, Tony Blair's proposal to move CAP funds to cognitive-technology R&amp;D). Seillière's preface to *Les Dirigeants face au changement* introduced the volume in which Patrick Le Lay explains selling "available brain-time". The rhetorical question: is Medef's re-enchantment a "jumpstart" of spirit, or industrial knowledge *without* spirit? Ars Industrialis is defined as "an international association for an industrial politics of technologies of spirit". Ecological and civilizational stakes: Laurence Tubiana is quoted, though the translation spells her "Toubiana"; Robert Lyon's "age of less"; survival requires overcoming the "age of consumption" through "new, qualitative growth".

## Short quotations

- Arthur on *esprit*: it "expresses a synthesis of the psychic and social, as well as intellectual and historical life of man" (p. viii).
- Introduction: capitalism "called sometimes 'cultural,' sometimes 'cognitive,' but that is before all else the destructive organization of an industrial populism" (p. 1).

## Notes for evaluation

- **Accuracy:** primary text, authoritative for structure and pagination. Note small typos in the English: "contra" for *contre* and "le valeur" for *la valeur* in the preface; "Steigler"; "savior-faire"; "it's lowest point". These suggest light copy-editing. The French cover's attribution to Ars Industrialis is dropped from the English title page, which matters for questions of authorship (see [STRUCTURE.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/STRUCTURE/index.md>)).
- **Bias:** the translator's preface interprets as well as translates. Its framing in terms of drives versus desire and the "elixir" of *politesse* is Arthur's gloss.
- **Reliability:** high. The sample runs to about 12 pages of the book's text.

# French back cover, dedication, and Ch. 1 §3 (French edition)

A primary text, transcribed by an amateur reader with interpolated comments marked "hcq". Character encoding is damaged (accents dropped). It gives the French edition's paratext and Ch. 1 §3. **No continuous text is reproduced here.**

## What it establishes

- **French back cover (4e de couverture).** It is essentially a compressed version of the Introduction's opening: Valéry 1939; 45% radio listenership in 1939, no TV; communicating objects chasing "available brain time" from waking to sleeping; "cultural"/"cognitive" capitalism as the ravaging organization of **industrial populism** reducing the seat of spirit to a reflex organ, "a brain without consciousness"; Medef's 2005 summer university under the banner of re-enchanting the world; "this book proposes to take it at its word". It names **Georges Collins, Marc Crépon, Catherine Perret and Caroline Stiegler** as co-founders of Ars Industrialis with Stiegler.
- **Dedication (French ed.).** "To the memory of Simon Nora. To Laurence Parisot." Nora co-wrote the 1978 Nora–Minc report *L'informatisation de la société*, which Ch. 2's first section title echoes. Parisot became Medef president in July 2005, succeeding Seillière.
- **French pagination anchor:** Ch. 1 §3 runs at **pp. 42–47** of the French first edition, against English pp. 31–33.

## Condensed account of Ch. 1 §3 (our paraphrase)

1. No one decides how they live. We reproduce ways of life inherited from family, adopted through education, or taken from foreign cultures through trade, migration, evangelization, new techniques, ideologies and culture industries. **Individuation is essentially a process of adoption** (cross-reference to *Technics and Time 3*, ch. 3).
2. Civilizations form by inventing ways of life that others adopt and by adopting others'. Examples: China, unified over about three millennia with written characters as an Asian form of **hypomnemata**, now itself a new capitalism that may export its way of life through service industries; Alexander adopting Egyptian religion and having Egyptians adopt his, as shown by an Alexandrian tomb combining Persephone/Hades with Isis/Osiris.
3. A society's future lies in adopting new ways of life, including new technologies and above all hypomnemata. But adoption carries a future only if it strengthens or creates a process of **psychic and collective individuation**, so that adopters can individuate *themselves* and intensify their singularity, their **negentropic** potential.
4. **Hyperindustrial capitalism**, as now organized, does the reverse. It **takes control of adoption at every level**, starting with primary and secondary **identification** (cross-reference to *Mécréance et discrédit 2*, *La Télécratie contre la démocratie*). This **destroys individuation**, psychic and collective. As a **service capitalism** using ICTs as technologies of **control** rather than individuation, it generalizes **proletarianization**: producers lose *savoir-faire*, consumers lose *savoir-vivre*. Life loses its taste. There is a play on *savoir*/*sapere*/*sapide*: knowledge makes the world savoury, and a world needs *savoir-vivre*, an art of living, civility, *politesse*.
5. Definition: the proletarian is one who loses their knowledge. The producer becomes pure labour power; the consumer, whose *savoir-vivre* has become a user manual, becomes pure purchasing power. Just as "cognitive capitalism" (Negri to Seillière) and "knowledge society" (Blair, UNESCO, Serres) are announced, capitalism liquidates knowledge, produces **entropy** and disgust, and makes the world insipid. Cognitive industries do to knowledge what culture industries did to the arts, turning them into entertainment or "mass mystification" (citing Marc Jimenez, 2006 seminar).
6. Jimenez's analysis lacks a projection into the dynamics of **grammatization** and a **general organology** (defined in a note: the joint evolution of physiological organs, artificial organs and social organizations, in Simondon's transductive relations). Such an approach would show both the necessity of this stage and its alternatives. Still, an **enslaved spirit** (*esprit asservi*), a servile spirit serving service societies, produces generalized malaise and self-disgust. Hyperconsumption is only a seemingly paradoxical symptom (notes cite the Ars Industrialis session "Souffrance et consommation", 25 Feb 2006, and attack Lipovetsky's *Le Bonheur paradoxal*). The malaise in civilization has become the malaise of **consumption**, leading to a generalized refusal of the ongoing transformation, "especially in France".

## Notes for evaluation

- **Value:** the French text of a Ch. 1 section. Lotz's citation "enslaved spirit" (p. 33 English) belongs here. It also shows the chapter's notes are dense with cross-references to Stiegler's 2001–2006 books.
- **Reliability:** the transcription is partial and garbled, and mixed with the site owner's comments. Use for orientation, not quotation.

# Lemmens, interview with Stiegler, *Krisis* (2011)

Published in *Krisis*; a copy is at edepot.wur.nl/194315. The piece has two parts: Lemmens's introduction (secondary, pp. 33–35) and the interview itself (primary-parallel). Lemmens's introduction says Ars Industrialis "has published two manifestos and two books". *Réenchanter le monde* (2006) is one of those books, but the introduction does not name it.

## Condensed account

**Lemmens's introduction (pp. 33–35)** - **Two strands.** Lemmens places Stiegler in two lines: a Heideggerian rethinking of philosophy's forgotten technical condition (the *défaut d'origine*), and a continuation of critical theory, namely the critique of political economy and of the culture industry. He calls the second the "Marxist strand". - **Proletarianization.** Following Simondon and Marx, it is the loss of knowledge and know-how. Nineteenth-century capitalism proletarianised workers and twentieth-century capitalism proletarianised consumers, replacing their ways of life with marketed "lifestyles". Service-economy consumers are "discharged" of responsibility for their lives and lose savoir-vivre and joie de vivre. The claim that we live in a "knowledge society" is called a lie. - **Hyperindustrial society.** The systematic industrialisation of memory and cognition through digital technologies amounts to "hyperindustrial" societies, in which the life of the mind is industrialised. - **Psychopower.** On the analogy with Foucault's biopower, psychopower captures attention and desire. It ends in the destruction of libido and of sublimatory capacity, and it yields "systemic carelessness" and "systemic stupidity". Lemmens ties this to neoliberal, short-termist speculative finance. - **Contribution.** Digital networks may catalyse the passage from consumer society to a "society of contribution". Ars Industrialis is glossed as an "association for the promotion of an industrial politics of spirit".

**Interview (pp. 35–41)** - **No technological determinism.** There is a "technological condition" and a "general organology" of the psychic, technical and social. Technics is always in excess of society, which produces "disadjustment". - **Pharmakon.** It is poison at first. It becomes curative only through a second "epochal redoubling", in which society appropriates the new technical system (p. 36). - **Proletarianization.** It begins with technical exteriorisation itself, and Plato is its "first thinker". The question is whether exteriorisation produces autonomy or heteronomy. Kant's "minority" amounts to self-proletarianisation through reading without thinking (pp. 37–38). - **Neoliberal turn.** Thatcher and Reagan (1979–80) handed the socialisation of technics, previously done by state, school and church, to marketing. This produced speculative rather than investment capitalism ("mafiazation"), pp. 38–39. - **Libidinal economy / addiction.** "No pleasure produced anymore by the system". Consumers are addicts who know consumption is bad for them. Juliet Schor's survey is cited (p. 40). - **Contribution.** The question is not "the end of capitalism" but "a new industrial model". Free software, peer-to-peer and changes to property law break the 20th-century opposition between production and consumption. Stiegler is pragmatic about Open Source compromises (pp. 39–41).

## Short quotations

- Stiegler: "there is no technological determinism. What there is is a technological condition." (p. 36)
- Stiegler: "the process of proletarianization marks the beginning of humankind" (p. 37)
- Stiegler: "Because there is no pleasure produced anymore by the system." (p. 40)
- Stiegler: "The question today for me is not the end of capitalism or the return of the communist horizon. Today we have to create a new industrial model." (p. 39)

## Notes for evaluation

- **Value:** a clear oral restatement of the core programme of *Réenchanter* and the manifestos, covering the industrial model, Ars Industrialis, the opposition between production and consumption, and libidinal exhaustion, in accessible English. The p. 39 statement is a useful primary answer to the Marxist critics (Hutnyk, Manche): Stiegler explicitly brackets the question of whether the new model will still be capitalism.
- **Lemmens's stance:** sympathetic, reading Stiegler through critical theory and Heidegger. Lemmens later pursues an eco-Marxist and Sloterdijkian line, but here he presses Stiegler on the neoliberal "strong state" and on the marginality of Free Software, which makes the interview usefully probing.
- **Caveat:** the interview postdates the book by four years and uses the post-2008 pharmacology vocabulary.

# Stiegler, Ars Industrialis session of 24 September 2005 (Théâtre de la Colline)

Stiegler's talk to the Ars Industrialis session of 24 September 2005, and the precursor of Chapter 2. The printed chapter keeps the talk's section skeleton and core theses but is **substantially expanded**; see [chapters/05](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/chapters/05-ch2-against-the-reign-of-ignorance/index.md>) §"What changed from the 2005 talk". The talk is in 16 numbered sections. Sections 2 and 4–16 have headings that correspond **one-to-one and in the same order** to the 14 section headings of Chapter 2 in the English edition (pp. 61–94); compare [STRUCTURE.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/STRUCTURE/index.md>). Section 3 has no counterpart heading in the chapter. Its material on Medef/Kessler/Seillière reappears in the book's **Introduction** (pp. 2–3). The talk's purpose was to gather material for the motion before the Tunis WSIS (see [primary-arsindustrialis-tunis-motion-2005.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/primary-arsindustrialis-tunis-motion-2005/index.md>)). Christian Lotz's page references show material not in the talk, e.g. Wikipedia at p. 87 and judgement at pp. 70–72. So this talk must not be treated as identical to the chapter.

## Section correspondence

| Talk § | Talk heading (FR) | Book Ch. 2 section (EN, p.) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Rappel sur les objectifs… | — (procedural; dropped) |
| 2 | De « l'informatisation de la société » à la « société de l'information » | From the "informatization of society" to the "society of information" (61) |
| 3 | L'esprit comme objet de lutte, ses nouvelles formes d'hypomnémata, le « réenchantement du monde » et l'Europe | ≈ From the "information society" to "societies of knowledge"—or, on the possibility of "re-enchanting the world" (64) |
| 4 | Entreprises, vision à long terme, nouvelle puissance publique et populisme industriel… | Enterprises, public power, and industrial populism (66) |
| 5 | Le temps est venu de changer les axiomes du paradigme industriel | Changing the industrial paradigm (70) |
| 6 | Société de l'information, désenchantement, démotivation et contrôle des savoirs | Information society, disenchantment, demotivation, and the control of forms of knowledge (71) |
| 7–8 | Instrumentation et instrumentalisation des savoirs; Société hyperindustrielle et renaissance des savoirs | The re-instrumentation of forms of knowledge and the future of hyperindustrial society (73) |
| 9 | Savoir et information | Knowledge (Savoir) and information (77) |
| 10 | Savoir et mémoire, ou règne de l'ignorance ? | Knowledge and memory, or reign of ignorance? (79) |
| 11 | Le risque de la désindividuation | The risk of disindividuation as the growth of ignorance rather than knowledge (81) |
| 12 | Saturation cognitive et knowledge management… | Cognitive saturation and "knowledge management" (83) |
| 13 | Les instruments du savoir et les critères de sélection… | Instruments of knowledge and the criteria of selection that they produce (87) |
| 14 | Être et devenir dans la « technoscience » | Being and becoming in "technoscience" (89) |
| 15 | La crise écologique de l'esprit se traduit d'abord comme une crise de l'éducation | The crisis of education (90) |
| 16 | Conséquences pratiques | Practical consequences (91) |

(3→64 and 7–8→73 correspond by content; the rest match heading for heading.)

## Condensed account (our paraphrase, by section)

- **§2 Informatization → information society.** The "information society" grew out of e-commerce, disintermediation, tax avoidance and globalization's *remote control* (Boltanski &amp; Chiapello). UNESCO's "knowledge societies" and "cognitive capitalism" name the same thing. Its roots are civilian networking from 1992 (TCP/IP; Clinton–Gore "information superhighways") and generalized digitization. That went far beyond the 1978 Nora–Minc report on the "informatization of society". In the 1990s audiovisual, IT and telecoms **converged**. The result is what Ars Industrialis calls **technologies of spirit**, which for now feed Valéry's "drop in the value of spirit", a **desublimation** (in a sense different from Marcuse's).
- **§3 Spirit as stake of struggle.** Tunis is about spirit as the **power to sublimate** and socialization as sublimation, always within a **libidinal economy** and always through **hypomnemata**. Digitization has created new forms of them. The struggle is a reversal: what now lowers the value of spirit could raise it. Kessler glossed Medef's "re-enchantment" theme this way, citing Blair on moving CAP money to knowledge technologies. Seillière's preface to *Les dirigeants face au changement* speaks of human capital and the knowledge economy. The question is geopolitical: what would make a specifically **European** political economy of technologies of spirit, and could that re-enchant the European project?
- **§4 Enterprises and industrial populism.** Against Medef, the firm is *not* the agent of this change. First, Seillière's "continuous adaptation" ends grand industrial strategy. Stiegler argues (*Constituer l'Europe 2*) that adaptationism is an **entropic vicious circle** that breeds **demotivation**. Industrial policy for technologies of spirit must be **long-term** and run by a **new international public power** with private actors. Second, the existing organization produces generalized debasement, a true **industrial populism**. The proof is that the same Seillière-prefaced book contains Patrick Le Lay's (TF1) statement that what TF1 sells Coca-Cola is "available human brain time".
- **§5 Change the axioms of the industrial paradigm.** Brain time made available this way is the worst case of the **society of control** (Bradbury/Truffaut's *Fahrenheit 451*). Le Lay boasts of next-day audience data and calls *Star Academy* "controlled reactivity". A real knowledge society raises everyone toward refined forms of spirit through **works of sublimation**. The contradiction between Seillière's call for social intelligence and Le Lay's organized stultification requires a **change of axioms**. These changes should be the agenda of Tunis and of Barroso's Lisbon strategy.
- **§6 Disenchantment, demotivation, control of knowledge.** Medef can talk of enchantment because the economy is **libidinal**. Spirit is a matter of *motives* (motivation) and so of **psychic and collective individuation**. Cultural/cognitive capitalism brings Weber's disenchantment to a head and is a stage of **grammatization**. It controls knowledge of production and of consumption through R&amp;D, design and marketing. Theses: (a) a new instrumentation of research produces an **entropic** tendency against the **negentropic** nature of knowledge; (b) it coincides with losses of *savoir-faire* and *savoir-vivre*; (c) these are losses of individuation, singularity and desire; (d) an **industrial ecology of spirit** is needed.
- **§7 Instrumentation vs instrumentalization.** All knowledge requires *instrumentation*, a "techno-logic", and industrialization of instruments is not denounced. Today's fact is **instrumentalization**, and a *right* must be opposed to that fact. Control technologies of **societies of control** (Burroughs/Deleuze) are the condition of future individuation. Mesopotamian and Egyptian control technologies became, as hypomnemata, the basis of **Greek individuation** and the citizen.
- **§8 Hyperindustrial society and renaissance of knowledge.** Hyperindustrialization is unavoidable but has **self-destructive limits**. A **renaissance of knowledge** through instrumentation is the condition for crossing them, a "sustainable development of spirit". This requires digital instruments that are true **technologies of intellect**. Current models of industrial innovation are incompatible with the value of spirit.
- **§9 Knowledge vs information.** Information as commodity is **entropic**: its value decays with time. Knowledge is **negentropic**: it keeps and intensifies its value, and it constitutes time. Lyotard (*The Postmodern Condition*): knowledge produced to be sold loses its use-value, "a doing without knowing". This is an internal contradiction of ICT-based knowledge societies. There is no spirit without a **material milieu** (Husserl's *Origin of Geometry*, Leroi-Gourhan, Goody). Against Michel Serres: externalization does not free us from memory to devote us to knowledge. **Externalization of memory is the origin of the human** and the condition of knowledge, and it is a process of **grammatization**.
- **§10 Memory, or the reign of ignorance?** One need not follow Plato's *Phaedrus* in opposing living *anamnesis* to written *hypomnesis*. Living memory must project itself outside to overcome its retentional finitude. The real threat is **externalization without correlative interiorization** (= individuation). The **school** is the institution for appropriating the alphabetic hypomnesis. A knowledge society that fails to organize social appropriation of the new hypomnesic devices, through a European **politics of technologies of spirit**, would become a new **reign of ignorance**. "Anamnesic capacity" names knowledge's negentropy, its "revenance" (Husserl on reactivating the origin, as with Euclid in Lobachevsky).
- **§11 Disindividuation.** Informationalization is both a threat and a chance. Digital convergence merges conception, production and consumption into one cognitive system, while children's "available brain time" is captured during the years meant for education. So the knowledge-society question is first about **television** and its relation to digital media, and it requires public policy. Individuation is always psychic *and* collective: knowledge is knowledge only when shared and public. The risk is not loss of memory but loss of individuation, an entropic collapse arising from unresolved conflict among the **psychic, collective and machinic**.
- **§12 Cognitive saturation and KM.** "Cognitive overflow syndrome": information accumulates as unprocessable data instead of becoming knowledge. **Knowledge-management** tools are managerial ("cognitive" meaning decision-supporting), not scientific. Tools for teaching and research are spin-offs of the tertiary sector, and e-learning has been disappointing or regressive. Real knowledge markets are "insolvent", and public authorities have stopped underwriting them.
- **§13 Instruments of knowledge and their selection criteria.** Following Auroux, the alphabet is **grammatization** preceding all logic and science. The third industrial revolution moves from **mnemotechnical** to **mnemotechnological** societies, where cognitive functions are delegated to machines and production absorbs the clerks. Memory, including information about the present, becomes the object of vast **industries of memory and imagination** separating producers from consumers. Memory is retention and therefore **selection**. Industrializing it means imposing new **criteria of selection** (Google's challenge to Europe). An instrument of knowledge produces its own selection criteria as its practical rules. An **ecological crisis of spirit** is possible because spirit is originally externalized and so exploitable. The aim is to subordinate the organization of information to the imperatives of knowledge.
- **§14 Being and becoming in technoscience.** Technoscience constantly calls being into question and abandons knowledge's ontological project. Schools teach that knowledge formalizes what *is*, while knowledge now explores *becoming*. Axiomatic and axiological crises (e.g. in biology) make transmission nearly impossible, so teachers lag structurally behind what pupils meet daily. Condorcet, Guizot and Ferry did not think from originary externalization.
- **§15 Crisis of education.** Stiegler's reading of Kant (*Technics and Time 3*) argues the transcendental deduction ignores a "fourth", **prosthetic synthesis** of imagination. Program institutions (education systems) are therefore helpless before **program industries**. The ecological crisis of spirit shows first as an **educational crisis**, and also as a crisis of knowledge-producing institutions. A new instrumental chain of knowledge (**digital instrumentality**) can and must be oriented by **public policy**.
- **§16 Practical consequences.** Knowledge instruments must be specific, hierarchized and reversible, not sub-applications of office software, document management or KM. Production tools must suit users' qualifications. Dissemination tools should share their basic functions so that recipients can retrace the genesis of statements. A publishing industry for knowledge societies should serve the institutions that prescribe programs. Priorities: (1) new instruments for research and higher education; (2) new editorial functions for schools. This is feasible: computer-assisted intellectual work (annotation, criticism, argument, indexing, synthesis) is technically mature; discretizable and delinearizable audiovisual "temporal objects" can de-massify audiences (INA 1997 studio, IRCAM music education); hypertext enables **societies of authors and readers**, contrary to dominant business models.

## Short quotations

- Knowledge "is by essence negentropic", whereas commodified information "is by essence entropic" (§9, our translation).
- The danger is a society of non-knowledge, "a new age of the reign of ignorance" (§10, our translation).

## Notes for evaluation

- **Reliability as a proxy for Ch. 2:** high for the argument skeleton, moderate for detail. The book version adds material. Lotz's citations show pp. 68 ("total absence of thought"; spirit as capacity to imagine alternatives), 70–72 (one's own and critical judgements), 75 ("collective intelligence") and 87 (Wikipedia). Those are not in this talk.
- It contains a long Le Lay quotation sourced to *Les dirigeants face au changement* (Éditions du Huitième jour, 2004), p. 92. This is the standard citation for "temps de cerveau humain disponible".
- Footnotes reference Stiegler's contemporaneous books: *Constituer l'Europe* 1–2 (2005), *De la misère symbolique* 1 (2004), *Mécréance et discrédit* 1–2 (2004–6), *La technique et le temps* 3 (2001). Ch. 2 condenses their arguments.

# Stiegler, "Economizing means taking care" (2008)

A web essay. No translator is credited on the page, and the text has no pagination. Hutnyk (2012) cites it as the epigraph source for "psycho-power" (see lit-hutnyk-proletarianisation-2012.md).

## Condensed account

- **Care / economy.** "Economy" is taken in its etymological sense of the household: to economise is to take care. Attention is both psychic and collective, and paying attention means taking care. An industrial system could be a system of care, with care as its value chain, instead of consuming its own resources.
- **Psychopower.** It is the systematic capture of attention by psychotechnologies (radio, TV, digital). Marketing is its organ, it succeeds Foucault's biopower, and it destroys the identification between parents and children. The counter-concept is a "noopolitics" built on "technologies of spirit" that support sublimation.
- **Libidinal economy.** Consumerism channels libido into drives that destroy their objects, whereas desire cares for and sustains its object. The capitalist libidinal economy therefore "self-destructs".
- **Three limits of capitalism.** These are the falling rate of profit, the destruction of libidinal energy, and environmental toxicity. Rifkin's hydrogen economy is insufficient if it ignores libidinal energy. The same three-point scheme appears in the Ars Industrialis "Mécroissance" entry.
- **Proletarianization.** It affects producers and consumers alike. The production/consumption opposition is its structural cause, and overcoming it is the key to any exit from crisis. (Contribution is implied but not elaborated on this page.)
- **Short-termism.** Speculative finance indifferent to its objects, and a short-term way of life, destroy the capacity for long-term projection, which the ecological crisis requires.
- **Pharmacology.** Tertiary retentions can heal or harm. Every attentional technology can be reversed to dissociate attention, and social networks can build or short-circuit collective individuation.
- **Otium / skholè.** "Ascendant" innovation coming from users is linked to skholè and otium (leisure devoted to knowledge and the art of living), set against the production/consumption model.

## Short quotations (Stiegler)

- "to economise is to take care"
- "Psycho-power is the systematic organisation of the capture of attention"
- "the capitalist libidinal economy self-destructs"
- "The loss of attention is a loss of capacities of projection into the long term"

## Notes for evaluation

- **Relation to the book:** this is the closest freely available English text to *Réenchanter*'s programme. It shares the call for a European industrial politics of "technologies of spirit", the diagnosis that the consumerist libidinal economy is self-destroying, and the link between the investment of capital and libido. It is later (post-2008) and adds the pharmacological and psychopower vocabulary, along with the 2008 crisis.
- **Reliability:** an authorial text, so authoritative for Stiegler's views. The English is unattributed and unpaginated. Cite with the date caveat.

# Stiegler, "L'avenir du capitalisme" (Libération diary, June 2005)

A week of diary entries in *Libération*, written in the founding weeks of Ars Industrialis, just after the French "no" to the European Constitutional Treaty (29 May 2005).

## Condensed account (the opening of each entry)

- **Sat 11 June, "Beautiful Europe and its libido".** American reports of lost libido are set beside a former Jospin adviser, now Orange strategist, celebrating mobile-phone "coaching". We exist only by expressing ourselves to others: the gift/counter-gift circuit of **symbolic exchange**. The culture industry has ruined it, collapsing libido and motivation and destroying aesthetic participation (Leroi-Gourhan: "one must participate in order to feel"). Aesthetic participation contains political participation (Aristotle's *philia*). The 29 May "no" is read as a sudden protest by the unheard against this **symbolic misery**.
- **Sun 12 June, "Prayer for newspapers".** The journal was first a private diary supporting **otium**, then a public organ through which a group individuates as opinion. Reduced to information it now denies opinion and destroys individuation. Richard Durn (the 2002 Nanterre shooter) wrote a diary about needing to do harm to feel he existed. Freedom passes essentially through *otium*.
- **Mon 13 June, "Flux of artifices".** Abstention of 57% in June 2004 prompted *Mécréance et discrédit 1*. Turnout of 70% on 29 May. Participation is linked to **otium**, which Stiegler equates with **spirit** (sacred or profane): time for care of self, self-cultivation and writing (Plutarch's *tekhnè tou biou*).
- **Tue 14 June, "New critique".** One year after *Les dirigeants face au changement*, Le Lay revealed that **industrial populism** is the principle of "cultural capitalism". Seillière's preface on the knowledge economy is quoted. If the knowledge economy is not a hollow slogan, television should become an organ for **elevating minds** rather than making people stupid by diverting libido. This motivates an industrial politics of technologies of spirit.
- **Wed 15 June, "Error and power".** The Daewoo fraud and Juppé's plan to sell Thomson Multimedia for one franc illustrate an internalized failure to believe in public–private industrial strategy, which affected the French Socialists too. Hence the need for a **new form of public power**.
- **Thu 16 June, "Enlightened capitalism".** Strategy begins by identifying the enemy. It is not Islamism, sovereigntism, nationalism or political populisms as such, but **desublimation**, the result of **industrial populism** (Le Lay and "enemies of the beautiful", or with Kant and Lyotard, of the sublime). An **enlightened capitalism** must put an end to it.
- **Fri 17 June, "Europe, this young girl".** Returns to 29 May as a democratic question.

## Notes for evaluation

- It shows that by June 2005 the book's key vocabulary was already in place: industrial populism, desublimation, Le Lay/Seillière, new public power and "enlightened capitalism". The vocabulary was public before the French book (October 2006).
- It shares vocabulary with Ch. 1's European theme ("A European way of life", pp. 53–58) and the "jumpstart" (*sursaut*).
- The phrase "enlightened capitalism" supports critics (Lotz; Radical Philosophy's "technoreformism") who read Stiegler as reformist. See [reception.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/reception/index.md>).

# Stiegler, "Pharmacology of Desire" (2011)

An article by Stiegler in *New Formations*. Page numbers are the journal's.

## Condensed account

- **Libidinal economy and psychopower (pp. 150–151).** The starting point is Edward Bernays, Freud's "double nephew" and the inventor of public relations and so of marketing. Twentieth-century libidinal economy was transformed by marketing into a **psychopower**, the counterpart of Foucault's biopower. Psychopower channels consumers' libido toward commodities so that industrial investment can return a profit.
- **Subsistence, existence and consistence (p. 151).** The "historicity of the unconscious" lies in the relation between an economy of subsistence (needs), an economy of existence (desires), and "consistences" (objects of idealisation). The present crisis is the collapse of the consumerist arrangement between these, through the liquidation of consistences, that is, of sublimation.
- **Disposability (p. 151).** Consumerism is an economy of disposability and "infidelity": objects must be disinvested as soon as they are invested. Its counterpart is speculative finance (hedge funds, LBOs), which is structural disinvestment. This drive-based consumption links to **short-termism**.
- **Organology (pp. 152–155).** Freud's "organic repression" (upright stance, olfaction) is reread with Leroi-Gourhan as prosthetic de- and re-functionalisation. There is "no libido without aesthetics", and the libidinal aesthetic is "pros-thesic". Political, symbolic and libidinal economy form three levels of general organology.
- **Transindividuation (pp. 156–158).** Superegoic and sublimatory "retentional systems" depend on intergenerational long circuits of transindividuation, which psychotechnologies short-circuit. The result is regressive identification (Freud's *Massenpsychologie*) and "generalised proletarianisation", that is, loss of savoir-vivre and systemic "dis-apprenticeship". Long circuits are modelled on the Socratic dialogue and anamnesis.
- **Associated vs dissociated milieus (p. 158).** Associated milieus are transitional milieus (Winnicott) in which participants co-individuate their milieu. The opposition between producers and consumers of symbols "de-symbolises" consumers, who no longer take part in shaping their milieu. Dissociated milieus are therefore toxic and dis-individuating. This is the conceptual core of **symbolic misery**, although the term itself is not used.
- **Le Lay (p. 159).** Psychotechnologies standardise secondary retentions. That is what Le Lay called selling "available brain time" to Coca-Cola.
- **Libidinal ecology (p. 159).** Drive-based capitalism is "addictogenic": consumers' addiction forms a system with speculators' "ultra-short-termist" behaviour.
- **Investment and money (pp. 159–160).** Investment is both libidinal (binding drives over time) and capitalist (a system of protentions). Money is a tertiary retention and protention, and a pharmakon: it turns belief into trust (calculability), and that calculability ruins trust.
- **Disenchantment (p. 160).** Weber's secularisation and disenchantment has reached "extreme disenchantment". In this limit, three limits of capitalism potentise one another: the falling profit rate, falling libidinal energy, and negative externalities. A new pharmacology (digital) opens the possibility of reconstituting associated milieus.
- **Bêtise / Marcuse (pp. 160–161).** Generalised proletarianisation leads to "systemic stupidity", or *bêtise systémique*. The difference from Marcuse is that Marcuse wants to "liberate the instincts", whereas Stiegler holds that the artefact (pharmakon) conditions desire itself. Fuller treatment is referred to *Mécréance et discrédit 3: L'esprit perdu du capitalisme* (2006).

## Short quotations (Stiegler, trans. Ross)

- "consumerism is an economy of disposability, that is, of infidelity." (p. 151)
- "There is no libido without aesthetics" (p. 152)
- "Consumers are de-symbolised because they no longer participate in any way in the emergence of their transitional milieu" (p. 158)
- "an extreme limit in which three limits of capitalism combine and potentise one another" (p. 160)

## Notes for evaluation

- **Relation to the book:** this is the most compact free English statement of the libidinal-economy thesis that runs through *Réenchanter* (desire as capitalism's energy, the exhaustion of libido, Le Lay, the need for investment rather than speculation). It explicitly links that thesis to Weber's disenchantment ("extreme disenchantment"), so it is valuable for the re-enchantment slug. Its companion volume, *L'esprit perdu du capitalisme*, appeared in the same year as *Réenchanter*.
- **Vocabulary drift:** the systematic pharmacology and "dis-economy" language is post-2008, as in *Ce qui fait que la vie vaut la peine d'être vécue* (2010).
- **Reliability:** authorial and authoritative, with a peer-reviewed venue and a careful Ross translation that keeps the French glosses.

# Stiegler, "The Uncontrollable Societies of Disaffected Individuals" (2006; *Nordic Journal of Aesthetics*, 2013)

The *Nordic Journal of Aesthetics* text on "the lowering of the spirit value". It is a 2006 text, written at the same time as *Réenchanter le monde*, and it names Medef's 2005 summer university.

## Condensed account

- **Spirit (p. 129).** The text opens: "Symbolic misery leads irresistibly to spiritual misery." *Esprit* is a "noetic process that is both psychic and collective (cerebral and social)". It is what connects the I to the we, the "and" of psychic and collective individuation, "just as is, moreover, technics". It is not "vapour" or pure form. It passes through the organisation of matter. Knowledge (*connaissance*) is spirit's refined fruit, resting on savoir-faire and savoir-vivre. The translator's note (n. 1) says *esprit* means both mind and spirit, with no "vaporously 'spiritual'" sense.
- **Proletarianization (pp. 129–130).** Simondon held that the worker-become-proletarian is disindividuated. Stiegler extends this to consumers' savoir-vivre, which gives "generalized proletarianization". He doubts that industrialised cognitive technologies still yield individuation even in science.
- **Spiritual misery (p. 130).** It is the blockage of the psychic and social circuits that constitute objects of spirit (objects of admiration, sublimation and love). It produces anxiety, regression to drives and addictions, "panic" (herd reactions) and the "reign of stupidity". This is "the lowering of the spirit value, *la valeur esprit*" (Valéry), and ultimately despair (*dés-espoir*), the destruction of Kant's kingdom of ends.
- **Disenchantment (pp. 130–131).** Weber's disenchantment carries a becoming-reactive and stupid, which is Nietzsche's nihilism. It also carries "the potential for an unprecedented trans-formation", a "new epoch of the spirit". Carried to extremes, it lets capitalism conquer the world but leads to "the loss of the capitalist spirit". Against Boltanski and Chiapello, there is no "new spirit of capitalism": capitalism is threatened by itself. That is why **Medef took "the re-enchantment of the world" as the theme of its 2005 summer school** (p. 131).
- **Industrial populism (p. 132).** The loss of spirit "massively" takes the form of industrial populism: the exploitation of "available brain time", targeting drive-based and regressive mechanisms, against spirit understood as care for the objects and subjects of desire, including children. It destroys shame (*aidos*), the superego and sublimation, and leads to cynicism, acting out and "negative sublimation" (terrorism). This is cross-referenced to *Constituer l'Europe 1*.
- **Hyper-industrial society (pp. 132–133).** "Absolute disenchantment" is the loss of every horizon of expectation, of belief and of *philia*, especially for those who expect nothing from "hyper-industrial society". The hyper-power of the technical system depends on trust and turns into hyper-vulnerability once trust is lost.
- **Attention and control (p. 133).** Industrial populism arises from the destruction of attention through control technologies, above all TV (Deleuze, Daney). Control of primary and secondary identification by industrial temporal objects leads to dis-identification and collective disindividuation. The result is "disaffected" individuals, in both senses: affect is ruined (*désaffection*) and their place, their ethos, is lost (*désaffectation*).

## Short quotations (Stiegler, trans. Ross)

- "Symbolic misery leads irresistibly to spiritual misery." (p. 129)
- "spirit is what exceeds the I and connects it to the we, the condition of the 'and' of psychic and collective individuation" (p. 129)
- "Disenchantment, when carried to extremes, may have allowed capitalism to conquer the entire world, but it eventually leads to the loss of the capitalist spirit." (p. 131)
- "This loss of spirit above all takes the form, massively, of industrial populism, the exploitation of 'available brain time'" (p. 132)

## Notes for evaluation

- **Relevance:** very high. It is contemporaneous (2006) and runs the exact chain of the book: symbolic misery, then spiritual misery and the fall in the value of spirit, then disenchantment, the loss of capitalism's spirit, Medef's "re-enchantment", and industrial populism and "available brain time". It is the best free primary text for checking how the book uses *esprit* and *populisme industriel*.
- **Translation:** Ross's translation and note on *esprit* (mind and spirit) are useful to compare with Trevor Arthur's choices in the Bloomsbury book.
- **Reliability:** authorial and published, though only an excerpt (pp. 129–134).

# Barker, "Enchantment, disenchantment, re-enchantment" (New Formations 77, 2012)

An article in the *New Formations* special issue on Stiegler. The issue editorial (Gilbert and Roberts, pp. 5–6) introduces it.

## Condensed account

1. Since co-founding Ars Industrialis in 2005, Stiegler has moved toward the political side of critical theory. *Réenchanter le monde* (2006) and *Prendre soin (1) de la jeunesse et des générations* (2008) are presented as his two most dynamic recent works in this direction.
2. The book addresses a culture that has lost its sense of history in a "hyper-technical age". It proposes a politics of critique that accepts the technological world and seeks to restore *anamnesis*. It discusses "telecracy", agri-business, the culture industry and the political process, using a revised notion of *grammatisation*.
3. **Barker translates two sections of *Réenchanter le monde*, with extended commentary:**
4. "Grammatisation and Individuation Yesterday, Today, and Tomorrow". This corresponds to EN Ch.1, "grammatization and individuation", p. 47.
5. "The Risk of Disindividuation as the Increase of Ignorance Rather Than Knowledge". This corresponds to EN Ch.2, "disindividuation", p. 81.
6. Simondon's transduction and individuation, and *Technics and Time*, serve as the critical frames. Barker compares the "crisis of individuation" with *Taking Care*, which he translated for Stanford University Press.
7. The issue editorial says Barker's essay "explores the political implications" of *Taking Care* and *Réenchanter le monde*. It credits him with the phrase that Stiegler promotes "a critical politics vital to the twenty-first century".

## Short quotations

- (editorial, quoting Barker) "a critical politics vital to the twenty-first century"

## Notes for evaluation

- This was the **first English translation of parts of Ch.1 and Ch.2**, before Arthur's 2014 version. Arthur's headings are "Grammatization and individuation—yesterday, today, and tomorrow" (p. 47) and "The risk of disindividuation as the growth of ignorance rather than knowledge" (p. 81); Barker has "increase" where Arthur has "growth".
- Stance: sympathetic, Simondonian and deconstructive. Useful as a second English translation of these two sections.

## Notes for evaluation

- **FR/EN structural differences:** (1) The **2010 Manifesto** is an English addition; the 2006 French edition predates it. (2) There is no translator's preface in French. (3) The Eyrolles listing nests "Grammatisation et individuation" under "Le sursaut : entreprendre autrement", whereas the English contents list both as flat sections. (4) "Le **plan** qui m'enchante" becomes "the **plane** that enchants me": a correct rendering, since the section is about a plane of consistencies.
- The French edition prints the **Tunis motion** at FR p. 163 (cited in Ch. 2 n. 6). English publisher copy describes it as "an account of the organisation's 2005 summit in Tunis".

# Cherrier, lelitteraire.com (2012)

A short French web review of the 2006 Flammarion edition (172 pp., €12).

## Condensed account

1. Opens with Valéry's 1939 remark, made as Nazism advanced, on a "baisse de la valeur esprit".
2. The book's question is what place spirit and reflection have in industrial capitalism and in a consumer society saturated by communication technologies.
3. Innovation serves mass communication, which raises the question of whether spirit serves technology or technology serves spirit. The reviewer links this to loss of individuation and gives reality TV (*Star Academy*) as an illustration.
4. Nanotechnologies, RFID, the web, ADSL and Wi-Fi produce constant information. The reviewer paraphrases the book's claim that the result is a paradoxically "disinformed" society bathed in ignorance, which echoes Ch.2's information-versus-knowledge theme.
5. The book examines spirit's role in the economy and in a "European way of life" (cf. EN Ch.1 §"a European way of life", p. 53). Through Ars Industrialis it invites reflection with Arendt's "life of the mind" in view.
6. Its vocabulary (*hypomnémata*, *épokhal*, *pharmaka*) is an obstacle.
7. Verdict: relevant but hard going. Suited to philosophy students and specialists, and general readers should learn the terminology first.

## Short quotations

- "Un essai pertinent mais difficile d'accès"
- "une société finalement désinformée, baignant dans l'ignorance"

## Notes for evaluation

- Accurate but brief and impressionistic. There are no page references and no structural description. The *Star Ac* example may be the reviewer's own rather than the book's.
- Stance: a neutral general reader. Its complaint about difficulty agrees with Lyons, the SensCritique reader and Lotz.
- Low weight. Useful only as a sign of French lay reception.

# de Beer, Tydskrif vir Geesteswetenskappe (2012)

This is a review-article, not a short book review. It takes *Réenchanter le monde* (2006), rendered in Afrikaans as *Heropluistering van die wêreld: geestelike waarde teenoor industriële populisme*, as its "guiding publication". It reads the book together with the two Ars Industrialis manifestos and Stiegler's other books of 2004–2010.

## Condensed account

1. **Starting point.** The core message is to recover spirit, spirituality and the value of spirit. Disenchantment amounts to a *sociopathology* that calls for a *sociotherapy*, and that therapy depends on the activity of spirit.
2. **What "spirit" means.** It does not mean religious spirit. It is the defining human trait, a translation of Greek *nous*, meaning the living body as minded, knowing and relational. De Beer stresses that Stiegler leans on Valéry ("La crise de l'esprit", "La liberté de l'esprit") and places the book in the French *philosophie de l'esprit* tradition (Blondel, Lavelle, Le Senne, Bergson), alongside Malabou's materialist Hegel.
3. **Technologies of spirit (book pp. 27–28, within the Manifesto).** Culture industries, programme industries, media, telecommunications and cognitive technologies are converging into "technologies of spirit". These require an "industrial ecology of spirit" that takes in new social practices as well as calculation, and could found a "new epoch of civilisation" (p. 28).
4. **Industrial populism (book p. 9).** The authors point to factors that speed up humanity's decline. De Beer groups these as industrial populism: hyperindustrialism, hyperconsumerism, the dismissal of knowledge as a waste of time, the "whatever / so-what" attitude, Lacan's "will to ignorance", manipulation in place of noetic commitment, and "hyper-technicism".
5. **Two chapters.** The book gives two chapters to (a) the thorough *re-foundation of society* and (b) the *struggle against the reign of ignorance*. This matches EN Ch.1 and Ch.2.
6. **Knowledge without spirit? (book pp. 13–14).** Is knowledge produced through industrialised savoir-vivre, savoir-faire and savoir-penser, and through cognitive technologies, really individuation of the contemporary episteme, given "cognitive saturation" and an "entropy" of hypotheses, axioms and methods? Can knowledge without spirit be knowledge? This page range is probably in the Introduction. The cognitive-saturation theme is developed in EN Ch.2 at p. 83.
7. **Being vs having.** The book quotes Robert Lyon (*Le Monde*, 7 July 2006) on the "century of less": humanity can come out of this only by siding with *being* rather than *having*. De Beer gives no page.
8. **Pharmakon (book p. 82).** Cited together with Manifesto 2010 point 4 for the claim that digital technics is a pharmakon and that "nootechnics" or technologies of spirit can be turned toward cure.
9. **Manifestos.** He quotes Manifesto 2005 point 7 (English 2008 web version): an industrial politics of spirit needs a new form of public power that brings together economic actors, institutions, researchers, artists, philosophers and investors. He quotes Manifesto 2010 point 6 for the definition of proletarianisation as loss of formalised knowledge. His bibliography places the "Manifeste d'Ars Industrialis" at **pp. 27–35 of the French edition**, and says the same journal issue carries an Afrikaans translation of the 2005 manifesto.
10. **Conclusion.** A "polemology" (struggle) for spirit leads to a sociotherapy or "nootherapy": re-founding a true "we", fighting ignorance as a fight for intelligence, reinventing care and love, re-enchanting the world, and recovering "nearness of being".

## Short quotations

- (English abstract, de Beer's words) the aim is "a reinvention of spirituality and the re-enchantment of the world"
- (abstract) "Nothing less than a socio-therapy will suffice."

## Notes for evaluation

- **Usefulness.** This is the only source found that gives **page references to the French edition**: pp. 9, 13–14, 27–28, 82, and the Manifesto at pp. 27–35. French pagination does not match EN. FR Manifesto pp. 27–35 corresponds to EN pp. 11–16.
- **Caution.** Many of de Beer's other page references (2006a, 2006b, 2006c) are to *Mécréance et discrédit* 2 and 3 and *La télécratie contre la démocratie*, not this book. A bare "(p. 93)" quotation about consumers "dispossessed of all knowledge" is ambiguous and should not be attributed to *Réenchanter*.
- **Stance.** Strongly sympathetic and somewhat homiletic. It reads Stiegler through a quasi-spiritualist and Heideggerian lens (being, nearness of being, Fromm's *To Have or To Be*) and adds Ubuntu-adjacent communal language. It plays down the political-economy and libidinal-economy material and does not treat the Tunis motion.
- **Contrast.** Roodt's article in the same issue (see review-roodt-…) disputes the Arendtian lineage of "spirit" that the Manifesto claims, whereas de Beer accepts the spirit vocabulary uncritically.
- **Reliability.** Good for structure and for FR page anchors. Its interpretation adds a good deal of de Beer's own material.

# Flammarion back-cover text (2006) and booksellers' summaries

The blurb as reproduced by Babelio (truncated), leslibraires.ca and SensCritique (short summary), homocoques.com (full blurb plus dedication and an extract, 19 April 2012), and the Philharmonie de Paris catalogue (summary). Below is a paraphrase, not the text.

## Condensed account

1. **Opening:** Paul Valéry, foreseeing where Nazism was leading, noted as early as 1939 a "baisse de la valeur esprit". That was a time when radio was little listened to and television did not yet exist. Today communicating devices capture "available brain time" (*temps de cerveau disponible*, Le Lay's phrase).
2. **Occasion:** the 2005 Medef summer university took "re-enchanting the world" as its theme. The book takes this at its word and argues that re-enchantment requires rethinking the place of spirit (*esprit*) in organising the economy.
3. **Thesis (leslibraires.ca and SensCritique):** Bernard Stiegler, president of Ars Industrialis, and the association's co-founders argue that the fall in the "valeur esprit" has become the very principle of capitalism. Facing coming civilisational and economic crises, they call for fighting the reign of ignorance and for an industrial policy of the "technologies of spirit", including media and television.
4. **Diagnosis (homocoques):** contemporary hyperindustrial capitalism treats the mind as a mere organ of reflexes, undermining thought and culture.
5. **Credits:** co-founders Georges Collins, Marc Crépon, Catherine Perret and Caroline Stiegler. The Philharmonie record notes that the volume includes the Ars Industrialis Manifesto.
6. **Dedication (homocoques transcription):** "A la mémoire de Simon Nora." / "A Laurence Parisot". Nora co-wrote the 1978 Nora–Minc report on the informatisation of society, cf.
