The lesson plan asks teachers to put Le Lay's sentence back in its context, an interview for the book *Les dirigeants face au changement*, using Acrimed's full reproduction (article1688). It also asks them to return to "le discours de Stiegler sur les pulsions, de vie et de mort", and asks what a "promesse sadique" is. The further reading includes Stiegler's *La Télécratie contre la démocratie* (2008).

## Short quotations

- The film is an effective indictment "notamment grâce aux réflexions du philosophe Bernard Stiegler".

## Notes for evaluation

- This is evidence of the **pedagogical afterlife** of the Le Lay and Stiegler pairing. The "available brain time" critique reached schools via the documentary, not via *Réenchanter le monde* itself, which the sheet does not cite.
- It is accurate on the Le Lay source (interview in *Les dirigeants face au changement*). It relies on Acrimed.

# Stiegler, "Cognitive technologies" (Ars Industrialis, 5 Nov 2005)

**Nature of source.** A written contribution (c. 2,600 words) posted for the session. The session page (node/1461) also lists contributions by Philippe Aigrain, Jean-Max Noyer and Alain Giffard, and links the Tunis motion.

## Condensed account

- **Origin of the concept.** Stiegler says he placed "cognitive technologies" at the basis of the Costech laboratory he founded at the Université de technologie de Compiègne in 1993. The aim was to distance it from cognitive science, which modelled cognition on an idealised Turing machine with infinite memory and ignored the role of tools and prostheses. His axioms are that every memory is finite and every machine is concrete. He compares this with Californian "situated cognition".
- **Memory theory.** As in *Technics and Time* 1, human knowledge appears with a third, external and technical memory ("epiphylogenetic") alongside genetic and somatic memory. "Tertiary retention" makes possible mnemotechnics, such as alphabetic writing as the condition of geometry, law and philosophy. Cognitive technologies are the latest **hypomnémata**. Together with the "cultural" technologies of communication, which are now merging with them through digitisation, they form the "technologies of spirit" of the Ars Industrialis manifesto. The example given is Mesopotamian catalogues as early "directories".
- **Practical experience.** He cites projects he worked on: a computer-assisted reading station for the Bibliothèque nationale de France, which was not completed because the BnF withdrew; an audiovisual reading station for the INA legal deposit; hypermedia documentary formats for digital TV; and aids for blind users.
- **Method.** Today "use" is prescribed by user manuals and marketing so as to maximise return on investment, which is almost the opposite of epistemic activity. Design should instead rely on **circles of practitioners**, whose knowledge forms a Simondonian "preindividual fund". It should treat feedback as the co-evolution of the instrument within a whole cognitive arrangement. This requires public power to accompany the time needed to build such arrangements.
- **Axioms.** "Lire, c'est écrire": perception requires motor action. Cognitive technologies are hypomnémata produced by **grammatisation** (discretisation of the continuous), and every grammatisation also produces **disindividuation**. "Désindividuations et nouvelles formes d'individuation" are the political stake, "l'objet d'une lutte politique et économique".

## Short quotations

- "toute mémoire est finie et ... toute machine est concrète" (axioms; ellipsis mine).
- "lire, c'est écrire".
- "Désindividuations et nouvelles formes d'individuation sont l'enjeu politique des formes contemporaines d'hypomnémata".

## Notes for evaluation

- It is useful background for ch. 2's sections on knowledge management, instrumentation vs instrumentalisation, and the call for a "knowledge editorial industry". The practical "specific, hierarchical, reversible" design principles of the 24 Sept talk are grounded here in Stiegler's own engineering projects.
- It is one of the few places where Stiegler explains the concepts behind the book in a talk setting and in a practitioner register (design methodology). It is self-presentational: the claims about Costech's priority and the BnF project come from Stiegler himself.

# Wikipedia coverage

**Is there a dedicated article?** No. Neither **Ars Industrialis** nor the **book** has a standalone Wikipedia article. Both are covered inside the Stiegler biographies.

## Condensed account

- **English Wikipedia, "Bernard Stiegler".** "In June 2005 Stiegler founded a political and cultural group, Ars Industrialis", whose manifesto calls for an "industrial politics of spirit". It names co-founders George Collins, Marc Crépon, Catherine Perret and Caroline Stiegler, and mentions an updated 2010 manifesto. **No inline citations** for these sentences. The bibliography lists *Réenchanter le monde* (2006) "with Marc Crépon, George Collins &amp; Catherine Perret" and the Bloomsbury 2014 translation. It does **not name the translator** and has no description of the book. IRCAM directorship is given without dates. Pompidou directorship of cultural development from 1 Jan 2006, and IRI created April 2006 (cited to the IRI site).
- **French Wikipedia, "Bernard Stiegler".** "En 2005, avec Marc Crépon, \[George Collins, Catherine Perret, Caroline Stiegler\] il fonde l'association Ars Industrialis", with a cited mission phrase "pour une politique industrielle des technologies de l'esprit". IRCAM director 2002 to 1 Jan 2006 (cited). The book is listed under "En collaboration" without a note. **No mention of the 2020 transformation** of the association, and no description of the book or of the Medef context.
- **French Wikipedia, "Temps de cerveau humain disponible".** A well-referenced article (L'Expansion, Nouvel Obs, Le Monde, Acrimed, *Communication &amp; langages*) on Le Lay's 2004 remark. It records Stiegler's reaction in *Le Monde diplomatique* (June 2005) and his role in the 2010 documentary. It is inconsistent about the source book's title (see [context-le-lay-temps-de-cerveau-2004.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/context-le-lay-temps-de-cerveau-2004/index.md>)).

## Short quotations

- EN: "In June 2005 Stiegler founded a political and cultural group, Ars Industrialis".

## Notes for evaluation

- **Authorship of the book.** EN Wikipedia lists three co-authors (Crépon, Collins, Perret) and omits Caroline Stiegler. The FR article lists four. Library catalogues (e.g. Philharmonie de Paris) credit "Bernard Stiegler et Ars Industrialis \[Marc Crépon, Georges Collins, Catherine Perret et Caroline Stiegler\]", and the Ars Industrialis site and the Tunis motion name the same five founders. **The EN bibliography's three-name list is an error or omission.** Mirrors of the 2006 Wikipedia text spread it further.
- "Founded June 2005" is consistent with the inaugural session of 18 June 2005, but it is uncited.
- The articles are adequate for basic facts and say nothing about the book's argument. Don't use them for content.

# Ars Industrialis: what the association's own site says

## Condensed account

- **Name.** "Association internationale pour une politique industrielle des technologies de l'esprit".
- **Self-description ("qui sommes-nous ?").** The page opens with a quotation from Demy's *Les Demoiselles de Rochefort* ("Nous sommes des sœurs jumelles…"). The founders describe themselves as "au départ quatre philosophes et une juriste", "cinq" at the initiative of the association. They are worried by the "désarroi" in industrial countries, especially France. Their working hypothesis is that a decisive element of the contemporary *malaise* (in Freud's sense) is a mutation in the **technologies of spirit**, the "hypomnémata" of our time (after Foucault's "L'écriture de soi"). They want to be a "force de proposition, et non seulement de réflexion". Thought and the life of the spirit consist first in **combating stupidity (bêtise)**, beginning with one's own, and the "forces of regression" that encourage it.
- **The founders** (from the inaugural minutes and the Tunis motion): **George Collins, Marc Crépon, Catherine Perret, Bernard Stiegler** (philosophers) and **Caroline Stiegler** (jurist).
- **Public sessions** were held at the Théâtre de la Colline (Paris), usually on Saturday afternoons, roughly quarterly. Up to the book's publication (Oct 2006) and just after: 18 June 2005 (inaugural); 24 Sept 2005 (knowledge vs information society: the Tunis summit); 5 Nov 2005 (cognitive technologies and digital libraries); 25 Feb 2006 (suffering and consumption); 20 May 2006 (politics and television); 14 Oct 2006 (public impotence and political power); 16 Dec 2006 (sustainable investment); 20 Jan 2007 (participatory democracy); May–June 2007 (formation and destruction of attention). A parallel seminar, "Trouver de nouvelles armes. Pour une polémologie de l'esprit", ran at the Collège international de philosophie for about four years.
- **2020\.** A convocation signed by Bernard Stiegler calls an extraordinary general assembly on **27 February 2020** to amend the statutes and found the "**Association des Amis de la Génération Thunberg**". It refers to the Internation group's work, presented in Geneva on 10 January 2020 to Antonio Guterres and Greta Thunberg. The site footer reads "arsindustrialis.org – 2008-2012". The site is now essentially an archive and links to "Épokhè".

## Short quotations

- "au départ quatre philosophes et une juriste".
- Thought "consiste d'abord à combattre. Combattre la bêtise, et d'abord sa propre bêtise".

## Notes for evaluation

- This is the authoritative source for the founders and the session chronology, and it settles the co-founder question (five people, including Caroline Stiegler). Compare [media-wikipedia-stiegler-ars-industrialis-2026.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/media-wikipedia-stiegler-ars-industrialis-2026/index.md>).
- everybodywiki ("Ars industrialis") claims the association was **renamed in 2017**. The association's own 2020 convocation points to a **2020** statutory change instead.
- The site is partisan by nature. It records what the association did, not how others received it.

# Le Lay: "Ce que nous vendons à Coca-Cola, c'est du temps de cerveau humain disponible"

## Established facts

- **Speaker.** Patrick Le Lay, then chairman and CEO (PDG) of the TF1 television channel. He died in March 2020.
- **Publication.** The remark appeared in an interview printed in ***Les Dirigeants face au changement*** (Paris: Éditions du Huitième Jour, 2004). This volume is a "baromètre 2004" by the partners of the consultancy **EIM (Executive Interim Management)**. It mostly contains interviews with French business leaders (the catalogue record says 21) and has a **preface by Ernest-Antoine Seillière**, then Medef president. French Wikipedia also gives the title as *Les Dirigeants français et le changement* (June 2004). The page is inconsistent on this point, and the form used by Acrimed, Stiegler and the Swiss teaching sheet is *Les Dirigeants face au changement*.
- **How it became public.** Acrimed reports an **AFP dispatch of 9 July 2004**, followed by a *Libération* item (10–11 July 2004) headlined "Patrick Le Lay, décerveleur". French Wikipedia cites *L'Expansion/L'Express* of 9 July 2004 as the earliest dated coverage, and *Le Nouvel Observateur*. In a September 2004 *Télérama* interview, reported by *Le Monde* on 8 Sept 2004, Le Lay said the Medef had invited him to a discussion about change, that it was not an official interview, and that the phrase was "un peu caricaturale et étroite".
- **Exact wording** (as reproduced by Acrimed). Key sentences:
- "à la base, le métier de TF1, c'est d'aider Coca-Cola, par exemple, à vendre son produit"
- "Or pour qu'un message publicitaire soit perçu, il faut que le cerveau du téléspectateur soit disponible."
- "Nos émissions ont pour vocation de le rendre disponible"
- "Ce que nous vendons à Coca-Cola, c'est du temps de cerveau humain disponible."
- "Rien n'est plus difficile que d'obtenir cette disponibilité." French Wikipedia also gives his remarks that audience share "se joue chaque jour" and that television is "une activité sans mémoire". Stiegler's 2005 talk, the precursor of ch. 2, quotes further lines from the same interview on reactivity (*Star Academy*). I have not checked whether the printed book keeps all of them.

## Stiegler's use

In the 24 Sept 2005 Ars Industrialis talk (see [primary-parallel-stiegler-colline-2005.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/primary-parallel-stiegler-colline-2005/index.md>)), Stiegler quotes Le Lay at length. He calls this business model **"industrial populism"** and says selling "available brain time" is the very opposite of a knowledge society. He also cites Le Lay on knowing audiences "to the second" and on *Star Academy* as "réactivité maîtrisée", and he links this to Bradbury and Truffaut's *Fahrenheit 451*. The Tunis motion (14 Nov 2005) defines "esprit" as both the "temps de cerveau disponible" that TV channels want and the source of "œuvres de l'esprit". French Wikipedia also says Stiegler called the remarks "effroyables de cynisme et de vulgarité" in *Le Monde diplomatique* (June 2005, "De la misère symbolique 2. La 'catastrophe' du sensible"). Stiegler also appears in the 2010 France 3 documentary *Le Temps de cerveau disponible* (Jean-Robert Viallet and Christophe Nick; see [media-plandetudes-fiche-temps-de-cerveau-2010.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/media-plandetudes-fiche-temps-de-cerveau-2010/index.md>)).

## Notes for evaluation

- The **date is often given loosely as "2004"**, and the publication varies between "a book" and "an interview". The precise form is an interview in an EIM book, publicised by AFP on 9 July 2004. Some English sources misdescribe it as a TV statement or a speech.
- The Medef link is real but is often missed: the volume was prefaced by Seillière, and Le Lay said the Medef asked him to take part. This is why Stiegler can join "re-enchantment" (Medef 2005) and "available brain time" (Medef-prefaced book, 2004) into one critique.
- Wikipedia's sourcing for the book title is internally inconsistent, as noted above.

# The Medef 2005 summer university ("Réenchanter le monde")

## What could be established

- **The theme.** The Medef (the French employers' federation) held its 2005 *université d'été* under the banner "Réenchanter le monde". Three sources support this. (1) Ars Industrialis's own presentation of its 24 September 2005 session says the Medef summer university "a mis son programme de rencontres sous le signe de la nécessité de 'réenchanter le monde'" (node/1460). (2) Olivier Ezratty, a tech consultant who attended the 2005 edition as a spectator, lists the sequence of Medef summer-university titles: "Réenchanter le monde" (2005), "Concilier l'inconciliable" (2006), "Jouer le jeu" (2007), "Voir grand" (2008). (3) The French publisher's blurb, quoted on bookseller and reader sites, says that in 2005 the Medef held its summer university "sous la bannière du 'réenchantement du monde'".
- **Who chose and framed it, according to Stiegler.** Stiegler's 24 September 2005 talk (node/1933; see [primary-parallel-stiegler-colline-2005.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/primary-parallel-stiegler-colline-2005/index.md>)) attributes the theme to **Ernest-Antoine Seillière**, Medef president until July 2005. He says **Denis Kessler**, a leading Medef figure, presented the theme by calling for an "âge d'une augmentation de la valeur esprit", that is, a greater role for knowledge in the economy. According to Stiegler, Kessler cited a **Tony Blair** speech proposing to redirect EU Common Agricultural Policy money towards knowledge technologies. Stiegler also cites Seillière's preface to the EIM volume *Les Dirigeants face au changement* (2004), the same book that contains Patrick Le Lay's "temps de cerveau humain disponible" remark (see [context-le-lay-temps-de-cerveau-2004.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/context-le-lay-temps-de-cerveau-2004/index.md>)). Stiegler suggests the preface may have been written by advisers or by Kessler. The book's Introduction repeats this material (English edition pp. 2–3, per the existing primary-parallel file). A French excerpt of the Introduction quoted on the Charybde blog (see [review-hugues-charybde27-2024.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/review-hugues-charybde27-2024/index.md>)) adds details. The theme served to promote the views of a Medef leadership "qui était alors en train de changer" on cognitive capitalism and knowledge industries. Kessler "en présentant cette université d'été" referred to Blair's proposal at a time when Britain held the EU presidency (second half of 2005). Seillière had himself wanted this summer university "juste avant de quitter la direction du Medef". The excerpt also sets out the book's question: is the Medef's re-enchantment a "sursaut de la valeur esprit", or a project for an industrial production of "connaissances sans esprit"?
- **Leadership.** Laurence Parisot succeeded Seillière as Medef president in July 2005, so the August 2005 summer university was held under her new presidency on a theme reportedly set by her predecessor. Her 2005–2013 tenure is confirmed by Wikipedia. According to a third-party transcription recorded in [review-flammarion-4e-de-couverture-2006.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/review-flammarion-4e-de-couverture-2006/index.md>), the French edition is dedicated "A la mémoire de Simon Nora" and "A Laurence Parisot". If that is correct, the book is pointedly addressed to the new Medef president.
- **Speakers.** Ezratty recalls being impressed by the speakers in 2005 and names only **Erik Orsenna** and **Canada's ambassador**, who spoke on state reform in Canada.

## What the Medef meant, as far as can be told

Every account available here comes through Stiegler or through readers repeating him. As he presents it, the Medef used "re-enchantment" as a positive slogan for the knowledge economy, the "société de la connaissance" of Blair and the Medef. Under that slogan, human capital and knowledge would replace the West's lost "technological rent" (Seillière's preface: "Ce début de siècle sonne la fin de la rente technologique pour l'Occident"). Stiegler and Ars Industrialis took the slogan "at its word" and turned it around. The same industrial milieu that wants re-enchantment also sells "available brain time", and that contradiction is the book's starting point. Stiegler set the slogan against Weber's "disenchantment" and Valéry's "baisse de la valeur esprit" (1939).

## Short quotations

- Ars Industrialis, presentation of the 24 Sept 2005 session: the Medef university placed its programme "sous le signe de la nécessité de 'réenchanter le monde'".
- Ezratty (2008): "'Voir grand' fait ainsi suite à 'Réenchanter le monde' (2005), 'Concilier l'inconciliable' (2006) et 'Jouer le jeu' (2007)."
- Kessler, as reported by Stiegler: "l'âge d'une augmentation de la valeur esprit".

## Notes for evaluation

- Kessler's and Seillière's statements are given here **through Stiegler's citation**, so they should be cited as "according to Stiegler".
- Ezratty's blog is a reliable first-hand record of the sequence of titles, but it is a personal blog.
- Do not confuse this event with other 2005–2007 "réenchantement" uses: Jean Staune's science and spirituality writing, Michel Maffesoli's *Le Réenchantement du monde* (2007), and Joshua Landy and Michael Saler's *The Re-Enchantment of the World* (Stanford, 2009). These are unrelated to the Medef event or to Stiegler's book.

# WSIS Tunis 2005 and the Ars Industrialis motion

## The summit (established)

- **What it was.** The UN World Summit on the Information Society (WSIS) ran in two phases: Geneva (December 2003) and **Tunis, 16–18 November 2005**. Tunisia proposed the summit, and the ITU adopted a resolution on it at its 1998 Minneapolis plenipotentiary conference (ITU French booklet). The ITU organised it under UN auspices.
- **Outcomes.** The **Tunis Commitment** (dated 18 Nov 2005) and the **Tunis Agenda for the Information Society**. These documents reaffirm Geneva's principles, address financing and the "digital divide", define Internet governance, and create the **Internet Governance Forum** (IGF), a non-binding multi-stakeholder forum. The US kept control of the DNS root zone and ICANN. Calls from Brazil, South Africa and China for multilateral (ITU) oversight ended in a vague compromise on "enhanced cooperation" (Wikipedia). Commentators said the summit made no notable progress on governance.
- **Attendance.** Wikipedia gives about 13,500 participants in total (c. 6,200 from NGOs, 4,800 from the private sector, 980 media). The ITU booklet gives no figures.
- **Controversy.** Tunisia under Ben Ali was criticised for its internet censorship and its treatment of journalists. RSF had protested the choice of host as early as 2002, quoting Robert Ménard: "il est tout simplement scandaleux de tenir un tel sommet dans ce pays". During the summit, according to Wikipedia, Ménard was refused entry, a *Libération* journalist was stabbed and beaten, a Belgian TV crew was forced to hand over footage, and a civil-society session ("Expression Under Repression") was obstructed.
- **Vocabulary.** UNESCO's preferred term was "knowledge societies" (plural, "sociétés du savoir"). The WSIS and EU term was "information society". Ars Industrialis exploited this distinction, and ch. 2 opens with it.

## The Ars Industrialis motion: how it came about (from arsindustrialis.org)

- **18 June 2005**, inaugural session (Théâtre de la Colline): knowledge societies and the Tunis summit were already on the agenda as the next topic (see [media-arsindustrialis-seance-inaugurale-2005.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/media-arsindustrialis-seance-inaugurale-2005/index.md>)).
- **24 September 2005**, session "Société de savoirs et société de l'information: les enjeux du Sommet de Tunis". It was moderated by Catherine Perret, with Jean-Max Noyer (Paris XI), Serge Regourd (Toulouse) and Stiegler (president). Its stated aim was to draft a public motion "en tant que personne morale" before Tunis. Stiegler's talk there is the precursor of ch. 2 (see [primary-parallel-stiegler-colline-2005.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/primary-parallel-stiegler-colline-2005/index.md>) and [media-arsindustrialis-presentation-tunis-seance-2005.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/media-arsindustrialis-presentation-tunis-seance-2005/index.md>)).
- **5 November 2005**, session on cognitive technologies and digital libraries, with contributions by Philippe Aigrain, Jean-Max Noyer, Stiegler and Alain Giffard. The page links to the motion text (see [media-stiegler-technologies-cognitives-2005.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/media-stiegler-technologies-cognitives-2005/index.md>)).
- **14 November 2005**: the motion "Le véritable enjeu du sommet de Tunis" was **published in *Libération***, two days before the summit opened. It was signed by George Collins, Marc Crépon, Catherine Perret, Bernard and Caroline Stiegler, "fondateurs d'Ars Industrialis" (full analysis in [primary-arsindustrialis-tunis-motion-2005.md](<https://lmmx.github.io/stiegler-reenchantment-of-the-world/sources/primary-arsindustrialis-tunis-motion-2005/index.md>)). It calls Tunis "le rendez-vous manqué" and asks for "un autre sommet". It criticises the Beffa report on industrial policy, commissioned by the French presidency, and the EU's Lisbon strategy (Barroso). It also demands that television become an instrument of knowledge rather than "industrial populism".

## Short quotations

- Tunis Commitment (French text): "Nous reconnaissons le rôle principal et les responsabilités des gouvernements dans le processus du SMSI."
- Ars Industrialis motion: "Le sommet de Tunis est le rendez-vous manqué de ces enjeux".

## Notes for evaluation

- **A common error, also in the Critical Inquiry review:** the motion is described as a "transcription of a group motion at the Tunis Summit". It was **not adopted at the summit**. It was a press motion by a small Paris association, published in *Libération* on the eve of the summit. The English title in the book ("A Motion Adopted by Ars Industrialis on the Eve of the Tunis Summit") is accurate.
- Some bookseller blurbs say the English edition includes "an account of the organisation's 2005 summit in Tunis". That is misleading: Ars Industrialis held no summit in Tunis.
